Pet Health
27.10.2026

### Chronic Kidney Disease in Cats — Symptoms, Stages, Treatment and Life Expectancy

Chronic kidney disease (CKD), often called kidney failure, is one of the most common illnesses of older cats. Studies suggest that 30–40% or more of cats over 10 years old have some degree of it, although in most of them it is still at an early, mild stage. The kidneys lose function slowly and permanently, and because cats are good at hiding illness, the first signs are easy to miss. But kidney disease is not an immediate death sentence: with early diagnosis, a renal diet and the right treatment, many cats live for years with a good quality of life. This article explains which signs to watch for, how the disease is diagnosed and staged, how we treat it at Saari Animal Clinic, what to do when a kidney cat will not eat, and what to expect.
Health
9.10.2026

### Senior Cat Health Check — What’s Included, How Often and Cost

A senior cat health check, or senior check-up, is a thorough examination with blood tests — ideally including a blood pressure measurement — that aims to find age-related disease before your cat shows clear signs. Cats hide illness well, and kidney disease, an overactive thyroid, high blood pressure, dental pain and arthritis often develop so slowly that owners put the changes down to “just getting old”. Feline guidelines advise regular check-ups for older cats, and at Saari Animal Clinic we recommend a senior check-up from about 7 years of age. It costs €299, or €309 with blood pressure measurement, which we especially recommend for cats.
Health
9.10.2026

### Dog Limping — When to See a Vet, Common Causes and Cost

Limping is a sign, not a diagnosis: something in the paw, leg, joint or spine hurts or is not working properly. Call a vet immediately, day or night, if your dog has been hit by a car or had a bad fall, if you suspect an adder bite, or if it suddenly cannot stand or walk. After hours, call the Northern emergency area’s on-call vet on 0600 399 299. See a vet the same day if your dog will not put any weight on the leg, has a fever or a hot, swollen joint, or is wobbly but still walking. If an adult dog has a mild limp but still bears weight on the leg and is otherwise well, you can keep it on strict rest for 24–48 hours; if the limp is not clearly better by then, book an examination. If a puppy or young dog limps, book an examination rather than resting it at home to wait and see.
Health
10.10.2026

### Ear Infections in Dogs — Symptoms, Causes, Treatment and Cost

An ear infection in dogs — inflammation of the outer ear canal, or otitis externa — is one of the most common reasons for a vet visit. The dog shakes its head and scratches its ears, and the ear smells bad or discharges. Do not wait for it to heal on its own: with proper examination and treatment, most acute ear infections clear within 2–4 weeks. A recurring infection almost always has an underlying cause, which needs to be found and kept under control. This article explains how to recognise an ear infection, what happens at the vet, what treatment costs at Saari Animal Clinic, and how to prevent it from coming back.
Emergency
24.9.2026

### Poisoning in Dogs and Cats: Symptoms, First Aid and When to Act Straight Away

Poisoning is a common reason for emergency visits to the vet. Often, a dog or cat is poisoned by eating something that is harmless to us but toxic to them, such as chocolate, xylitol or grapes — or by getting into human medicines. How ill the animal becomes depends on the substance, the amount swallowed and the animal’s size. A suspected poisoning is always worth an immediate call to your vet, even if your pet still seems perfectly well. For many poisons, treatment works best — or only works — before any signs appear.
Health
25.9.2026

### How often should a dog or cat be dewormed? Puppies, kittens, adults and travel

Modern advice in Finland is no longer to deworm every pet “just in case” several times a year. Parasite control is now risk-based: puppies, kittens and animals that hunt, roam or travel are dewormed on a schedule, while a healthy, low-risk adult can instead be checked with a faecal sample and treated only when needed. The idea is simple — treat at the right time and for the right reason, not by the calendar. Below are the current recommendations for cats and dogs of every age, based on the European ESCCAP guideline and Finnish practice. We also cover the signs of a worm infection, which product to choose, and the legal tapeworm treatment for travelling dogs.
Clinic
27.9.2026

### Veterinary Nurse — The Cornerstone of Patient Safety

A veterinarian who is operating cannot give the anaesthetic their full attention. A trained veterinary nurse watches the monitors, responds to changes and cares for the patient before, during and after surgery. In large studies, the main risk factors for anaesthetic death are the patient’s health before anaesthesia (ASA classification), age, body weight, and how major and how urgent the procedure is. These can rarely be changed on the day, but monitoring can: in cats, checking the pulse and using a pulse oximeter during anaesthesia have been linked to a lower risk of death. At our clinic, a trained nurse monitors the anaesthetic, so the veterinarian can concentrate on the operation.
Anesthesia
25.9.2026

### Hypothermia Prevention — Why Active Warming Matters

Hypothermia is one of the most common complications of anesthesia. In two Spanish studies, body temperature at the end of anesthesia was below 38.5 °C (the studies’ lower limit of normal) in 84% of dogs and 97% of cats, and below 36.5 °C in 32% of dogs and 71% of cats. Anesthetic agents impair the body’s temperature regulation, blood vessels dilate, and small patients lose heat rapidly. Hypothermia slows drug metabolism, prolongs recovery, and can impair blood clotting and heart function; in people, it also increases the risk of wound infection.
Anesthesia
24.9.2026

### Anesthesia Safety — Statistics, Risks, and How We Minimize Them

Anesthesia is an essential part of surgery, dentistry, and many diagnostic procedures. Many owners worry about it, and that is understandable. For a healthy dog or cat, however, the risk is low. In the large UK CEPSAF study (Brodbelt et al. 2008; 98,036 anesthetics and sedations in dogs and 79,178 in cats, 2002–2004), about 1 in 600 dogs (0.17%) and 1 in 400 cats (0.24%) died of causes related to anesthesia or sedation within 48 hours. For healthy patients, the risk was much lower: 0.05% (1 in 1,849) in dogs and 0.11% (1 in 895) in cats. A newer study (Redondo et al. 2024) of 55,022 anesthetics in dogs at 405 clinics and hospitals in 21 countries (general practices, referral practices, and university hospitals) reported a figure of 0.69%. The two figures cannot be compared directly, because the patients and the definitions differed.
Health
24.9.2026

### Vaccinations in Finland — Vaccination Program for Dogs and Cats

Vaccinations are the most effective way to protect pets from serious infectious diseases. In Finland, the Finnish Food Authority (Ruokavirasto) publishes vaccination recommendations. Apart from a few legal requirements (see Rabies and Travel below), they are not binding — the veterinarian always makes an individual assessment. The recommendations draw on the international WSAVA guidelines (2024); for cats, the Finnish feline medicine society Catus has adapted them to Finnish conditions.
Health
25.9.2026

### IBD or Lymphoma? — A Notoriously Difficult Differential Diagnosis in Cats

In cats, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and low-grade intestinal lymphoma are notoriously hard to tell apart. Both mainly affect middle-aged and older cats; low-grade lymphoma is very uncommon before 8 years of age. Signs include weight loss (the most common sign), vomiting, diarrhea, and changes in appetite. They can be mild, and diarrhea may be absent. The distinction matters because treatment and prognosis can differ: IBD is managed with diet and, if needed, corticosteroids, whereas low-grade lymphoma usually also needs oral chemotherapy.
Endoscopy
27.9.2026

### Gastroscopy — Stomach Examination and Foreign Body Removal with an Endoscope

Gastroscopy is an examination in which a flexible camera tube (endoscope) is passed through the mouth into the esophagus, stomach, and first part of the small intestine (duodenum). The vet sees the lining on a monitor, can take tissue samples (biopsies), and can often remove a swallowed object — without a surgical incision.
Dental
27.9.2026

### Tooth Resorption — A Hidden and Often Painful Dental Disease

Tooth resorption is a disease in which the body’s own cells (odontoclasts) gradually destroy the hard tissues of a tooth — cementum, dentin, and enamel. It usually starts on the root, below the gum line, and gets worse over time. It is most common in cats but is increasingly recognized in dogs. Once a lesion opens into the mouth, it is often painful — yet most affected cats show no obvious signs, so the disease easily goes unnoticed.
Cat Health
27.9.2026

### A Less Stressful Vet Visit for Your Cat — How We Help and How You Can Prepare

A vet visit is a stressful experience for many cats. An unfamiliar environment, strange smells, the presence of dogs and handling by strangers can trigger a strong stress response. Stress is not just uncomfortable — it also affects test results. In a study of healthy cats brought into an animal hospital, blood glucose rose above normal in most of them, with readings as high as about 18 mmol/L — values also seen in diabetic cats. Because of this effect, known as stress hyperglycaemia, a single high reading cannot, on its own, be taken to mean diabetes. Blood pressure is affected too: in healthy cats with implanted sensors, systolic pressure during a simulated clinic visit was, on average, about 18 mmHg higher than the cat’s own 24-hour mean, and the effect varied widely between cats and from one visit to the next. At Eläinklinikka Saari, we have invested in feline wellbeing and hold Silver-level accreditation in the international Cat Friendly Clinic programme.
Dental
27.9.2026

### Unerupted Teeth and Dentigerous Cysts — A Hidden Danger in the Jawbone

An unerupted tooth is a tooth that has never broken through the gum into the mouth — it stays hidden under the gum or inside the jawbone. Unerupted teeth are seen particularly often in brachycephalic (short-nosed) breeds. A fluid-filled dentigerous cyst can develop around the crown of an unerupted tooth and gradually enlarge, destroying the surrounding jawbone. Because the tooth cannot be seen, the problem often goes unnoticed until the damage is significant — unless dental X-rays are taken. At our clinic, we take dental X-rays and surgically remove unerupted teeth and dentigerous cysts.
Wildlife
25.9.2026

### Found a Baby Hedgehog? What to Do — A Finnish Guide

Every summer, people find a tiny hedgehog alone in the garden, on a path or out in daylight — and their first instinct is to scoop it up and help. Sometimes that instinct saves a life. Sometimes it accidentally orphans a healthy baby whose mother was only metres away. This guide will help you tell the difference, and show you exactly what to do — the Finnish way, and within Finnish law.
Wildlife
25.9.2026

### The Hedgehog in Europe and Finland — A Declining Garden Friend That Needs Our Help

The European hedgehog (Erinaceus europaeus) is one of our most beloved wild animals — and its numbers are falling across much of Europe. In October 2024, the IUCN moved the hedgehog from Least Concern to Near Threatened on its global Red List. Populations are thought to have shrunk in more than half of the countries where it lives. In many parts of its range, the decline appears to be approaching — or even exceeding — 30% over ten years, the threshold for a threatened category. In Finland, the hedgehog lives at the northern edge of its range, where long winters make survival especially hard. In this article, we look at the hedgehog’s situation, the threats it faces and how everyone can help.
Emergency
25.9.2026

### Pyometra in dogs — symptoms, how fast it progresses, treatment and recovery

Pyometra is a life-threatening infection in which the uterus of an unspayed female fills with pus. It is one of the most common serious diseases of intact bitches: roughly one in five unspayed female dogs (19–24% in Swedish insurance data) develops it by the age of 10. It also occurs in cats. The condition usually needs emergency surgery, and recognising the signs early can save your pet’s life. This article explains what the symptoms look like, how quickly pyometra develops, why antibiotics alone are not enough, how it is treated at Saari Animal Clinic, what recovery involves and how to prevent it.
Orthopedics
27.9.2026

### Lateral Suture — Cruciate Ligament Repair with Synthetic Support Material

Cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) rupture is one of the most common causes of hind-limb lameness in dogs; it is less common in cats. The lateral suture technique, also known as extracapsular lateral suture stabilization, is a well-established surgical method in which the knee is stabilized with synthetic material placed outside the joint. It is best suited to smaller and less active dogs, and it is also used in cats. At our clinic, the surgery is performed by veterinarian Pamela Kvarngård.
Pet Health
25.9.2026

### Chronic kidney disease (kidney failure) in dogs and cats — symptoms, stages, treatment and life expectancy

Chronic kidney disease (CKD), often called kidney failure, is one of the most common diseases of older cats: it may affect 30–40% or more of cats over 10 years old, although in most of them the disease is still at an early, mild stage. In dogs, it is much less common and is found mainly in older animals — in a large UK study, nearly two thirds of affected dogs were over 12 years old at diagnosis. The kidneys lose function slowly and irreversibly, and the first signs are easy to miss. But kidney failure is not an immediate death sentence — with early diagnosis and the right diet and treatment, many cats live for years, and dogs for many months to years, with a good quality of life. This article explains how to recognise the symptoms, what the IRIS stages mean, how we treat kidney patients at Saari Animal Clinic, what to feed, and what to expect.
Emergency
24.9.2026

### Adder Bite — Finland's Only Venomous Snake Bite in Pets

The European adder (Vipera berus) is Finland’s only venomous snake and lives across almost the whole country, including Ostrobothnia. Bites happen mainly from April to September, while adders are out of hibernation; in spring and autumn they often bask in the open on sunny slopes near their winter dens. Dogs are bitten most often because they sniff and paw at snakes, so most bites are on the head, muzzle or legs. Cats can be bitten too. An adder bite is always a veterinary emergency.
Pet Health
27.9.2026

### Food Allergies in Dogs and Cats — Symptoms, Diagnosis and Elimination Diet

Food allergy is one cause of itching in dogs and cats. In studies, it is found in roughly 15–20% of itchy pets — less often than environmental allergy (atopy). Many owners suspect grains, but the most common culprits in dogs are animal proteins such as beef, dairy products and chicken. Food allergy can only be diagnosed with an elimination diet and a food challenge, and we can help you with both.
Cat Health
30.10.2026

### Hyperthyroidism in Cats — Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment

Hyperthyroidism is the most common hormonal disease in older cats. Depending on the study, it affects up to about one in ten cats over 10 years of age. The overactive thyroid gland produces too much thyroid hormone (T4), which speeds up the metabolism and strains many organs, especially the heart and kidneys. Left untreated, the disease leads to serious complications. With treatment and regular check-ups, the outlook is usually good, although kidney disease found alongside it can affect the long-term prognosis.
Dental
27.9.2026

### PerioVive — Hyaluronic Acid Gel as an Add-On in Periodontal Disease Treatment

Periodontal disease is one of the most common diseases in dogs and cats: UK veterinary practices diagnose it in about 12.5% of dogs and 15% of cats in a given year, and detailed examinations under anesthesia find it in 44–100% of dogs. Left untreated, it can destroy the tissues that hold the teeth, causing bone loss and eventually tooth loss. PerioVive is a hyaluronic acid gel used as an add-on during dental procedures — not a stand-alone treatment.
Clinic
27.9.2026

### Why Choosing an Independent Veterinary Clinic Matters

In a 2024 report, the Finnish Competition and Consumer Authority (KKV) found that the Finnish market for small-animal veterinary care had concentrated heavily through acquisitions over the previous ten years and was led by two chains owned by foreign private equity investors — Evidensia and Vireä. Measured by 2023 revenue, Evidensia had 40–50% of the private small-animal market nationally and Vireä 10–20% (KKV gives ranges to protect business secrets). Eläinklinikka Saari is the only family-owned small-animal clinic in Vaasa, and we want to explain why that matters to us.
Dental
27.9.2026

### Tooth Brushing — The Best Thing You Can Do for Your Pet’s Teeth

Gum (periodontal) disease is one of the most common health problems in dogs and cats. Thorough examinations under anesthesia find at least early gum disease in most adult pets, often by two to three years of age. It causes pain and infection and has been linked to heart, kidney and liver disease. Daily tooth brushing is the most effective way to prevent it at home — and many pets learn to accept it.
Health
27.9.2026

### Grain-Free Food for Dogs and Cats — Is It Necessary or Harmful?

Grain-free pet food became a major trend, marketed as more “natural”. But in July 2018 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced an investigation into heart disease (DCM) in dogs eating certain foods, many of them grain-free. Here we review what the research shows — and what we recommend.
Health
25.9.2026

### Diarrhoea in Dogs and Cats — Causes, Home Care and When to Contact the Clinic

Diarrhoea is one of the most common reasons for a veterinary visit. Most cases are mild and settle within a few days — but diarrhoea can also be a sign of serious illness. Here is what causes it, how to care for your pet at home and when to contact the clinic.
Cardiology
27.9.2026

### Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) in Dogs — A Congenital Heart Defect That Can Usually Be Cured

Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is one of the most common congenital heart defects in dogs. The ductus is a blood vessel that connects the aorta and the pulmonary artery before birth; it should close soon afterward. If it stays open, it overloads the heart, and most untreated dogs develop heart failure within their first year or two. When PDA is found early and closed, it is usually cured.
Orthopedics
31.10.2026

### TTA Surgery in Dogs — Tibial Tuberosity Advancement for Cruciate Ligament Disease

Cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) disease is one of the most common causes of hind-leg lameness in dogs. The ligament usually weakens gradually and often tears partially before rupturing completely. The unstable knee is painful, and osteoarthritis develops in the joint. TTA (tibial tuberosity advancement) stabilizes the knee surgically without replacing the ligament.
Endoscopy
10.10.2026

### Ear Flushing Under Anesthesia (Video-Otoscopy) – Dogs and Cats

Ear infections are among the most common reasons dogs see a vet. A hand-held otoscope is enough for most ear examinations, but swelling and discharge can hide the eardrum. In video-otoscopy, a thin endoscope with a camera shows a magnified view of the ear canal on a monitor.
Anesthesia
25.9.2026

### Continuous Rate Infusion (CRI) — Steady Pain Management During Surgery

Pain management is one of the most important parts of any surgery. At our clinic, a pain-relief infusion is a routine part of larger operations, such as dog spays and orthopedic surgery. It is known as a constant rate infusion (CRI), also called a continuous rate infusion. Rather than relying only on separate injections, a CRI delivers pain medication into a vein at a steady, precisely controlled rate, usually after a starting dose. We start the infusion before the first incision and continue it throughout the operation.

# TTA Surgery for Cruciate Ligament Disease in Dogs

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/tta-surgery.html
Last updated: 2026-10-31

Orthopedics
31.10.2026

## TTA Surgery in Dogs — Tibial Tuberosity Advancement for Cruciate Ligament Disease

Veterinarian Pamela Kvarngård, Eläinklinikka Saari
Cranial cruciate ligament (CCL) disease is one of the most common causes of hind-leg lameness in dogs. The ligament usually weakens gradually and often tears partially before rupturing completely. The unstable knee is painful, and osteoarthritis develops in the joint. TTA (tibial tuberosity advancement) stabilizes the knee surgically without replacing the ligament.

### How Does TTA Work?

During TTA, the tibial tuberosity — the bony point below the knee where the kneecap tendon attaches — is cut and moved forward by an amount planned from X-rays. It is then fixed in its new position with a titanium cage and a plate secured with a fork and screws. As a result, the kneecap tendon runs at about 90 degrees to the joint surface at the top of the shin bone. This counteracts the force that pushes the shin bone forward when the dog bears weight (cranial tibial thrust). We also check the menisci (the knee’s cartilage cushions) and remove or treat a torn meniscus. At our clinic, TTA is performed by veterinarian Pamela Kvarngård, who has extensive experience in orthopedic procedures.
Side-view X-ray of a dog’s left knee after TTA surgery: the tibial tuberosity has been moved forward, a titanium cage holds the osteotomy gap open, and a plate secured with a fork and screws fixes the tuberosity in place. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.

### TTA or Lateral Suture?

We offer two surgical treatments for cruciate ligament disease: TTA and the lateral suture. The lateral suture stabilizes the knee with strong synthetic material placed outside the joint to mimic the ligament, whereas TTA permanently changes the forces acting on the knee. The lateral suture suits cats and small dogs, and often medium-sized dogs and older, calmer large dogs as well. TTA suits active dogs and large dogs. We always assess your dog individually to decide which method suits it best.

### Recovery

Your dog goes home with pain medication and a written home-care plan: leash walks only, with no running, jumping or free play until the bone has healed. Stitches come out at 12–14 days; a follow-up X-ray at 6–8 weeks checks bone healing before exercise is increased gradually. By 3–4 months most dogs walk with no limp or only a mild one, and improvement can continue for up to a year. We always recommend animal physiotherapy, which can speed recovery. An animal physiotherapist also sees patients at our clinic. In studies, about 9 in 10 owners rate the result as good or excellent.
Back-to-front X-ray of a dog’s left knee after TTA surgery: the cage in the osteotomy gap and the plate fixed with screws along the tibial crest. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Risks and Complications

Most studies report complications in about 1 in 10 to 1 in 3 dogs. Roughly 1 in 10 dogs has a more serious complication, often needing another operation, but most such problems can be treated successfully. Complications include infection, fracture of the tibial tuberosity or shin bone, implant failure, kneecap dislocation and a later meniscal tear (usually reported in 2–10% of knees). Osteoarthritis often still progresses over time, even after successful surgery. During surgery, we monitor anesthesia closely and give a multi-drug pain-relief infusion.

### What Does TTA Surgery Cost?

At our clinic, TTA surgery costs €1,703 for dogs under 20 kg and €1,803 for dogs over 20 kg. The price includes anesthesia, the surgery, medication and supplies, and stitch removal. Follow-up visits, such as the X-ray at 6–8 weeks, are charged separately. The final cost may be higher if additional examinations or treatment are needed. For comparison, lateral suture surgery costs €1,203 for dogs. Direct insurance billing is available for LähiTapiola, Agria and Pohjola customers. See our price list for current prices.

### When Should You Contact Us?

If your dog limps on a hind leg, has trouble rising or sitting, or is stiff after rest, cruciate ligament disease is a common cause. Partial tears usually progress, and delaying treatment raises the risk of meniscal damage, so do not wait. Roughly a third to a half of dogs with the disease in one knee later develop it in the other knee — older dogs less often. Keep your dog lean, as excess weight is a risk factor. Book an orthopedic examination and we will recommend the most suitable method.

# Ear Flushing Under Anaesthesia for Dogs and Cats – Price

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/video-otoscopy.html
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Endoscopy
10.10.2026

## Ear Flushing Under Anesthesia (Video-Otoscopy) – Dogs and Cats

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
An ear flush under anesthesia cleans the whole ear canal with a video-otoscope, so the eardrum can be checked and ear medicine reaches the skin of the canal. At Saari Animal Clinic in Vaasa it costs €449–489 depending on your pet’s weight (under or over 15 kg). Anesthesia and pain relief are included; microscopy of the ear samples is charged separately.
Ear infections are among the most common reasons dogs see a vet. A hand-held otoscope is enough for most ear examinations, but swelling and discharge can hide the eardrum. In video-otoscopy, a thin endoscope with a camera shows a magnified view of the ear canal on a monitor.

### Why Video-Otoscopy?

Thanks to far better magnification and lighting than a hand-held otoscope provides, even small eardrum tears can often be seen once the canal is clean. Fine instruments pass through the scope, so examination, sampling and treatment happen under a single anesthetic.
Video-otoscope image of a dog’s ear canal with otitis externa: the canal is packed with dark discharge and matted hair, and its wall is reddened. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### When Does a Dog or Cat Need an Ear Flush?

Most ear infections are diagnosed at an ordinary visit. Video-otoscopy is recommended when an infection keeps returning or resists treatment; the canal is blocked with discharge or the eardrum cannot be seen; or a foreign body (such as a grass awn), a growth, a ruptured eardrum or a middle-ear infection is suspected. In cats, it is also used to remove inflammatory polyps, benign middle-ear growths that can reach the ear canal.

### How Is the Ear Flush Done?

Badly swollen canals may first need 1–3 weeks of anti-inflammatory medicine. During general anesthesia with pain relief, a breathing tube protects your pet’s airway, because flushing fluid can drain through an open eardrum into the throat. The canal is flushed clean. Samples are examined under the microscope in our own laboratory and, when needed, sent for bacterial culture. Foreign bodies and polyps can be removed and growths biopsied. If the eardrum is intact but middle-ear disease is suspected, the vet may make a small opening in it (myringotomy) to sample and flush the middle ear. The opening usually heals within about five weeks if it is kept free of infection.

### Aftercare and Possible Side Effects

We give pain relief as needed and often leave a long-acting medicated gel in the cleaned canal. The procedure, especially opening the eardrum or removing a polyp, can cause head tilt and loss of balance, a drooping eyelid and a small pupil (Horner’s syndrome, more common in cats), facial paralysis or hearing loss. These signs usually pass within a few weeks but can be permanent. If you notice them, stop any ear drops and contact us the same day. In one study, polyps removed through the scope regrew in about one in seven cats.

### Chronic Ear Infections and Their Challenges

In dogs, recurring ear infections almost always have an underlying cause, most often allergy. Repeated inflammation narrows the canal, microbes shelter in a slimy biofilm, hard-to-treat bacteria such as Pseudomonas become more common, and the middle ear is often infected too. A flush clears the biofilm so medication reaches the skin of the canal, but the underlying cause must still be found and controlled.

### How Much Does an Ear Flush Cost?

At Saari Animal Clinic, an ear flush under general anesthesia with video-otoscopy costs €449–489, depending on your pet’s weight (under or over 15 kg). The price includes the anesthesia and pain relief. Microscopy of the ear samples, outside laboratory tests (bacterial culture, biopsies) and take-home medicines are charged separately. An ordinary ear examination with a sample checked under the microscope costs €137.79, including the visit fee. See our price list.

### When Should You Contact Us?

Book an appointment if your pet keeps scratching its ears or shaking its head, its ears smell or have discharge, or infections keep returning. Contact us the same day if your pet tilts its head or walks unsteadily, its eyes flicker from side to side, one side of its face droops, or it is clearly in pain. Call (06) 321 7300 or use our online booking. Read more: Ear Infections in Dogs.

# Ear Infections in Dogs – Symptoms, Treatment and Cost

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/dog-ear-infection.html
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Health
10.10.2026

## Ear Infections in Dogs — Symptoms, Causes, Treatment and Cost

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
An ear infection in dogs — inflammation of the outer ear canal, or otitis externa — is one of the most common reasons for a vet visit. The dog shakes its head and scratches its ears, and the ear smells bad or discharges. Do not wait for it to heal on its own: with proper examination and treatment, most acute ear infections clear within 2–4 weeks. A recurring infection almost always has an underlying cause, which needs to be found and kept under control. This article explains how to recognise an ear infection, what happens at the vet, what treatment costs at Saari Animal Clinic, and how to prevent it from coming back.

### What are the symptoms of an ear infection in dogs?

The most typical signs are head shaking, scratching the ears and rubbing them on the floor or furniture, a bad smell from the ear, yellowish, brown or dark discharge, redness of the ear canal and ear flap, and tenderness — the dog may yelp or pull its head away when the ear is touched. If the dog tilts its head or walks unsteadily, its eyes flicker from side to side, or one side of its face droops (lip, ear or eyelid), the inflammation may have spread to the middle or inner ear — see a vet the same day.
Otitis externa in a dog: the skin around the opening of the ear canal is widely reddened and scaly, with yellow-brown waxy discharge and crusts in the hair. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Why do dogs get ear infections?

The infection itself is almost always secondary: something else first inflames the ear canal, and yeast (Malassezia) and bacteria then thrive in the warm, moist, inflamed canal and keep the inflammation going. The most common underlying cause is allergy — environmental allergy (atopic dermatitis) or food allergy. In one study of 100 dogs with ear inflammation, allergic skin disease was the underlying cause in 43 of them. Other causes are ear mites, a foreign body such as a grass awn, skin scaling and oil-gland disorders (seborrhoea), autoimmune diseases, hormonal diseases such as hypothyroidism and, in older dogs, growths in the ear canal. Predisposing factors are floppy ears, narrow or hairy ear canals and moisture from swimming and bathing. Breed matters too: in a large UK study, Basset Hounds, Shar Peis, Golden Retrievers, French Bulldogs, Cocker Spaniels and Poodle crosses, among others, were at higher risk.
Otitis externa in a dog: the skin around the ear canal opening is red and moist, with dark brown crusted discharge and matted hair. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Does a dog ear infection heal on its own?

Do not count on it. An untreated or incompletely treated ear infection tends to become chronic: the skin of the ear canal thickens and scars, the infection can spread to the middle ear, and at worst the canal narrows so much that only surgery can help. Do not start ear drops at home on your own either — not even drops left over from an earlier infection. The wrong medicine does not work (an antibiotic, for example, does nothing against yeast), and some ear drops and cleaners can damage hearing and balance if the eardrum is ruptured, and only a vet can check whether it is. In Finland, veterinary ear medicines are prescription-only, and human ear drops are not meant for dogs. Ear cleaners are part of treatment, but on their own they do not cure an infection. If your dog is shaking its head or its ear smells, book an appointment — the earlier the infection is treated, the faster it usually heals.

### How is an ear infection examined and treated at the vet?

At the appointment the ear canal and eardrum are examined with an otoscope. A sample of the ear discharge is checked under the microscope right away in our clinic’s own lab: it shows whether there is yeast, bacteria, ear mites or a combination, so treatment is based on the finding, not on guesswork. The ear is cleaned and ear drops are prescribed, with antifungal, antibiotic and anti-inflammatory steroid components as needed; not every ear needs an antibiotic. If the infection keeps coming back or rod-shaped bacteria are seen, a bacterial culture and antibiotic sensitivity test may be needed. The first re-check is usually after 1–2 weeks, with the otoscope and a new sample. Treatment continues until the ear is clear — the disappearance of symptoms does not yet mean the ear is healthy. If the ear is very painful, the examination and cleaning can be done under sedation.

### When does a dog need an ear flush under anaesthesia?

If the infection is chronic or keeps returning despite treatment, the ear canal is blocked with discharge, or the eardrum cannot be seen, a more thorough examination is needed. At Saari Animal Clinic this is done with a video-otoscope under general anaesthesia: a thin camera shows a magnified image of the whole ear canal and eardrum on a monitor, the canal is flushed clean of discharge and bacterial biofilm, and samples can be taken and foreign bodies removed at the same time. Ear medication works only when it reaches the skin of the ear canal, so a clean canal is essential. Read more in our article Ear flushing under anaesthesia (video-otoscopy).
Video-otoscope image of a dog’s ear canal with otitis externa: the canal is packed with dark discharge and matted hair, and its wall is reddened. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### How much does treating a dog ear infection cost?

An ear-infection visit at Saari Animal Clinic: ear examination including sampling and microscopy €99.79 + visit fee €38, i.e. €137.79 in total. Ear drops and any other medicines sent home are extra. A re-check including a new sample and microscopy costs €77.88 + visit fee €38, i.e. €115.88 in total. A video-otoscopic ear flush under general anaesthesia costs €449–489 (anaesthesia and pain relief included; microscopy of the ear samples is extra). You will find our other prices in the price list. Direct insurance billing is available for LähiTapiola, Agria and Pohjola customers. An ear infection treated early is usually much cheaper than a chronic one.

### Why does a dog’s ear infection keep coming back?

When an ear infection keeps returning, ear drops only treat the consequence. The underlying cause is most often allergy, in which case the next step is an allergy work-up. Food allergy can only be diagnosed or ruled out with a strict elimination diet lasting at least 8 weeks, followed by a return to the old food to see whether the signs come back — blood tests are not reliable for this. Environmental allergy (atopic dermatitis) is diagnosed from the dog’s history and signs once other causes have been ruled out; allergy blood tests then help choose the allergens for immunotherapy (desensitisation). Allergy is usually lifelong but can be kept under control, often together with regular maintenance care of the ears. Other reasons for recurrence are hormonal diseases, structural changes in the ear canal and treatment that was stopped too early. We describe the work-up of recurrent infections on our Skin diseases, allergies and ear infections page.

### What happens when an ear infection becomes chronic?

Repeated rounds of inflammation and infection change the ear canal: its skin thickens, the canal narrows, and bacteria that resist many antibiotics, such as Pseudomonas, become more common. In long-standing ear inflammation the middle ear is often infected too, even when the eardrum looks intact. Chronic cases therefore often need a bacterial culture, a thorough flush of the canal under general anaesthesia and a long, closely monitored course of treatment. Most ear-canal surgery can be avoided if recurring infections are managed properly at an early stage. If the canal has become permanently narrowed and hardened (end-stage ear disease), however, the remaining option is surgery that removes the ear canal (total ear canal ablation).

### How do I care for my dog’s ears at home?

A healthy ear does not need regular cleaning — over-cleaning irritates it. After swimming or bathing, dry the ears and, if needed, clean them with an ear cleaner recommended by your vet: fill the canal, massage the base of the ear, and let the dog shake out the excess. Never insert a cotton bud into the ear canal — it pushes debris deeper and can damage the eardrum. Do not pluck ear-canal hair routinely: in a healthy ear, plucking can trigger inflammation, so ask your vet first. Dogs with recurring ear problems often need maintenance cleaning and anti-inflammatory ear drops on a schedule agreed with your vet. Check the ears weekly: a bad smell, redness or discharge is a sign that your vet should take a look.

### What about ear infections in cats?

In cats, ear inflammation is less common than in dogs, and the most frequent cause is ear mites (Otodectes cynotis), especially in kittens and young cats. The typical signs are dark, coffee-ground-like debris and intense itching. Ear mites are treated effectively with an antiparasitic, given to all cats and dogs in the household at the same time. A recurring or one-sided ear problem in a cat may be due to allergy or an inflammatory polyp — a benign growth from the middle ear, most common in young cats but possible at any age. In an older cat a tumour of the ear canal must also be ruled out, so a cat’s ear, like a dog’s, should always be examined.

### When does a dog ear infection need a vet?

Whenever the dog shakes its head or scratches its ears repeatedly, or the ear smells, discharges or is red and tender. Urgently, the same day, if the dog tilts its head or walks unsteadily, one side of its face droops, or it is clearly in pain. At Saari Animal Clinic in Vaasa we examine the ears with an otoscope and microscope at the same visit, and for chronic cases we have video-otoscopy and ear flushing. Book an appointment by calling (06) 321 7300 or via online booking.

# Senior Cat Health Check in Vaasa – What’s Included, Cost

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/senior-cat-health-check.html
Last updated: 2026-10-09

Health
9.10.2026

## Senior Cat Health Check — What’s Included, How Often and Cost

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
A senior cat health check, or senior check-up, is a thorough examination with blood tests — ideally including a blood pressure measurement — that aims to find age-related disease before your cat shows clear signs. Cats hide illness well, and kidney disease, an overactive thyroid, high blood pressure, dental pain and arthritis often develop so slowly that owners put the changes down to “just getting old”. Feline guidelines advise regular check-ups for older cats, and at Saari Animal Clinic we recommend a senior check-up from about 7 years of age. It costs €299, or €309 with blood pressure measurement, which we especially recommend for cats.

### What does the senior check-up at Saari Animal Clinic include?

The senior check-up takes about 30–45 minutes. We go through your cat’s eating, drinking, urination, stools and sleep, and any changes you have noticed. The veterinarian examines your cat thoroughly: heart and lungs with a stethoscope, abdomen and lymph nodes, mouth and teeth, eyes, ears, skin and coat, body condition, muscles and joints, and any lumps. A blood sample is sent to the IDEXX reference laboratory for the Geriatric Profile panel, which for cats includes:

#### Clinical examination

- Heart and lungs
- Abdomen and lymph nodes
- Mouth and teeth
- Eyes and ears
- Skin and coat
- Body condition, muscles and joints
- Lumps
- Eating, drinking, urination, stools and sleep — what you have noticed at home

#### Laboratory panel IDEXX Geriatric Profile

- Complete blood count
Kidney values 3
creatinine and urea, plus SDMA, an early marker of kidney disease
Electrolytes 6
sodium, potassium, chloride, calcium, magnesium and phosphate
Liver values 6
ALT, ALP, GGT, AST, GLDH and bilirubin
- Total protein, globulins and the albumin/globulin ratio
- Glucose and fructosamine, which helps tell diabetes from a stress-related rise in blood sugar
- Cholesterol, triglycerides, CK (a muscle enzyme) and T4 (thyroid hormone)
Blood pressure — measured calmly while your cat is awake, with cuffs sized for cats. Included in €309
Results are usually ready within a few days, and the veterinarian emails you a written summary: what looks good, what to monitor and concrete next steps.
Senior check-up
€299
With blood pressure
€309
Book online Call (06) 321 7300

### Why does my cat need a check-up if it seems healthy?

Cats are very good at hiding illness and pain — the AAFP Senior Care Guidelines name the cat’s “innate ability to hide ailments” as one reason why regular examinations matter so much in older cats. The diseases of old age also develop slowly: a cat drinks a little more, loses a little weight or jumps onto the sofa less often. Changes like these are easy to put down to age, but they are often the first signs of disease, and blood values can change before anything shows at home. Comparing results from year to year also reveals trends. A kidney value that is still within the reference range but higher than last year says more than a single number. Early diagnosis matters: in cats with established kidney disease, a kidney diet has been shown to reduce uraemic crises and lengthen survival.

### At what age is a cat a senior, and how often does it need a check-up?

The 2021 AAHA/AAFP Feline Life Stage Guidelines call cats aged 7–10 years “mature adults” and cats over 10 years “seniors”. Many age-related diseases, kidney disease among them, can begin before a cat reaches the senior stage, so we recommend a senior check-up from about 7 years of age. After that:
- Healthy older cats: once a year.
- Cats with a chronic disease (kidney, heart or thyroid disease, or diabetes): on a plan agreed with the vet, often every 3–6 months.

### Which diseases does a senior check-up look for?

The main age-related diseases in cats are:
- Chronic kidney disease — common in older cats, and it can begin in middle age; see Chronic kidney disease in cats.
- Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) — affects about 10% of cats over 10 years of age; see Hyperthyroidism in cats.
- High blood pressure — usually caused by kidney or thyroid disease (more below).
- Dental disease, including painful tooth resorption — the risk of both rises with age. Tooth resorption is easily missed in an awake cat, and confirming it often needs dental X-rays under anaesthesia.
- Osteoarthritis — degenerative joint disease affects up to 74% of cats aged 12 or older, yet many affected cats are never diagnosed or treated. Never give your cat human painkillers: paracetamol and ibuprofen are poisonous to cats.
- Diabetes — a common hormonal disease in senior cats.
- Heart disease — hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) affects an estimated 15% of cats overall and up to 29% of older cats. Many cats with HCM have no heart murmur. A normal examination does not rule it out; a heart ultrasound is the test for it.
- Weight and muscle loss — common in older cats, but unexplained weight loss always needs investigating.

### Which signs of illness in an older cat do owners often miss?

Watch for these small, gradual changes:
- drinking more, bigger clumps in the litter tray, urinating outside it, or constipation
- weight loss — especially if your cat is eating as well as before, or even more
- jumping less often or not as high, or hesitating before a jump
- a dull, unkempt or matted coat — a cat in pain grooms less
- yowling at night, being restless or seeming confused
- bad breath, drooling or pawing at the mouth
- hiding, sleeping more or losing interest in people and play
- eating less or vomiting more often
Night-time yowling, for example, can be caused by failing sight or hearing, cognitive decline, pain, an overactive thyroid or high blood pressure. Write down what you see, or film your cat at home: what you tell us is often as important as what we find in the examination. If you notice any of these changes, book an appointment — don’t wait for the next yearly check-up.

### Why should an older cat’s blood pressure be measured?

High blood pressure (hypertension) is much more common in cats over 10, and it often goes unnoticed until it has caused damage. In most cats it is caused by another disease; kidney disease and an overactive thyroid are the most common causes. According to the ISFM consensus guidelines, 19–65% of cats with chronic kidney disease, and 10–23% of cats newly diagnosed with hyperthyroidism, have high blood pressure. Untreated, it can damage the eyes, kidneys, heart and brain, and some of that damage may be permanent. Eye changes have been reported in about half of cats diagnosed with hypertension, and blindness caused by retinal detachment is often permanent. The guidelines recommend measuring blood pressure at least yearly in healthy cats aged 7–10, at least every 6–12 months from 11 years, and at least every 3–6 months in cats with kidney or thyroid disease. Stress can raise a cat’s blood pressure temporarily, so we measure it calmly while your cat is awake, using cuffs sized for cats. High blood pressure should be confirmed with repeated measurements, not diagnosed from a single reading.

### Does my older cat need a urine test too?

The AAHA/AAFP guidelines recommend a urine test as part of routine screening for cats aged 7–10, and strongly recommend it for cats over 10. It is not included in the €299/€309 senior check-up, so the veterinarian suggests one when it is useful — especially when kidney values are borderline or rising. Two results matter most:
- Urine specific gravity (USG) shows how well the kidneys concentrate urine. In cats, dilute urine can be an early sign of kidney disease, even while creatinine is still normal.
- Urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPC) measures protein leaking into the urine. The international IRIS guidelines use it, together with blood pressure, to classify kidney disease, and persistent protein loss is linked to shorter survival in affected cats.
A urine test also detects sugar in diabetes and evidence of urinary tract infection, which is more common in cats with kidney disease; a urine culture can find bacteria that cause no visible signs. If we recommend a urine test, you will get a clear price estimate first — nothing is done without your consent.

### How can I make the vet visit less stressful for my cat?

Saari Animal Clinic is an ISFM Cat Friendly Clinic at Silver level. In 2020 we became the first Cat Friendly Clinic in Ostrobothnia. Cats wait in an area screened from dogs, with raised shelves and covers for carriers, and are examined in a cat-only consulting room. Feliway diffusers in reception and the waiting area, and Feliway spray on tables and towels, help cats settle. We never scruff cats, and a cat in pain is given pain relief before the examination. Our cat advocate is Pamela Kvarngård. At home you can help:
- Leave the carrier out all the time, with the door open and soft bedding inside, so it becomes a familiar resting place.
- Spray Feliway into the carrier at least 15 minutes before your cat goes in, so the alcohol can evaporate.
- Cover the carrier with a towel and keep it stable in the car — on the floor behind the front seats.
- A carrier with a removable top is ideal: many cats feel safest in its bottom half.
For a very anxious cat, calming medication before the visit can be discussed with the vet in advance. Read more: A less stressful vet visit for your cat.
Listening to a cat’s heart on the examination table, right next to its own carrier. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### How much does a senior check-up for a cat cost?

At Saari Animal Clinic the senior check-up costs €299. This covers the veterinary visit, blood sampling, the IDEXX Geriatric Profile panel and the veterinarian’s interpretation of the results. With blood pressure measurement, which we especially recommend for cats, the price is €309. A dental check on its own, without anaesthesia, costs €32; during dental treatment under anaesthesia we usually also take full-mouth dental X-rays. If the check-up shows that further tests are needed — a urine test, dental X-rays or a heart ultrasound — you will get a clear price estimate first. A heart ultrasound (echocardiography) for a cat costs €376–476. It is done here at the clinic by our veterinarian Leena Sandström, a heart examiner authorised by the Finnish Kennel Club who holds an ESAVS cardiology certificate, so there is no need to travel to another city. See cardiac examinations. You will find our other prices in the price list.

### When should I take my older cat to the vet, and how do I book in Vaasa?

Book a senior check-up when your cat is about 7 years old, then once a year — or sooner if you notice any of the changes above. Some signs are emergencies. Call us straight away if your cat breathes fast or with effort at rest, suddenly cannot use its hind legs, or strains in the litter tray without passing urine (a blocked bladder, especially in male cats, and often mistaken for constipation). If your cat suddenly goes blind or has not eaten for more than a day, it also needs to see a vet the same day. Outside our opening hours, call the Northern emergency-area number 0600 399 299. You can book online or call us on (06) 321 7300. Choose a morning appointment and fast your cat for about 8–12 hours before the blood sample; water is fine, and give your cat its usual medication as normal unless agreed otherwise. If your cat has diabetes, agree with the vet in advance how to time food and insulin on the day.

# Dog Limping: When to See a Vet, Causes and Cost

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/dog-limping.html
Last updated: 2026-10-09

Health
9.10.2026

## Dog Limping — When to See a Vet, Common Causes and Cost

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Limping is a sign, not a diagnosis: something in the paw, leg, joint or spine hurts or is not working properly. Call a vet immediately, day or night, if your dog has been hit by a car or had a bad fall, if you suspect an adder bite, or if it suddenly cannot stand or walk. After hours, call the Northern emergency area’s on-call vet on 0600 399 299. See a vet the same day if your dog will not put any weight on the leg, has a fever or a hot, swollen joint, or is wobbly but still walking. If an adult dog has a mild limp but still bears weight on the leg and is otherwise well, you can keep it on strict rest for 24–48 hours; if the limp is not clearly better by then, book an examination. If a puppy or young dog limps, book an examination rather than resting it at home to wait and see.

### When should I take my limping dog to the vet?

Call a vet immediately, day or night — us on (06) 321 7300 during opening hours; after hours, the Northern emergency area’s on-call vet on 0600 399 299 — if your dog:
- has a leg that swells quickly — possibly from an adder bite, especially from April to September
- has been hit by a car or had a bad fall
- is bleeding heavily
- has a visibly deformed leg or a bone poking through the skin
- suddenly cannot stand or walk
- suddenly starts to drag its hind legs or knuckle over (walk on the top of a paw)
- has weak hind legs or back pain and suddenly cannot pass urine or control its bladder
- has sudden, severe back or neck pain — a hunched back, crying out when picked up, or the head held low
See a vet the same day — and call immediately if things get worse — if your dog:
- will not put any weight on the leg
- limps and has a fever or is lethargic, or has a hot, swollen joint
- has a limp that moves from leg to leg
- is wobbly but still walking
- has a bite wound or other open wound
If your adult dog has a mild limp but still bears weight on the leg and is otherwise well, keep it on strict rest for 24–48 hours: leash walks for toilet breaks only, no running, jumping or stairs. If the limp is not clearly better within 48 hours, gets worse or keeps coming back, book a lameness examination. If a puppy or young dog limps, book an examination rather than resting it at home to wait and see.

### What can I check at home when my dog is limping?

Start with the paw, gently and in good light — a dog in pain may snap, even at its owner. Check the pads for cuts. Spread the toes and look for thorns, splinters, grass awns or small stones and, in winter, balls of ice and irritation from road salt. Check every nail, including the dewclaw, to see if it is torn. Then run your hands down the whole leg, comparing it with the other side, and feel for swelling, heat or a spot that makes your dog flinch. Remove a thorn only if it is clearly visible and comes out easily, and leave anything embedded to the vet — a grass awn can work its way deeper into the paw. Never give your dog painkillers from your own medicine cabinet. Human anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen and naproxen can cause stomach ulcers, intestinal bleeding and kidney damage in dogs, so pain relief must always be prescribed by a veterinarian.

### Is my dog limping on a front or a back leg — how can I tell?

Watch your dog walk and trot on a flat, non-slippery surface. If a front leg is sore, the head rises when that leg touches the ground and drops when the healthy leg lands. If a hind leg is sore, the hip on the sore side rises as that leg takes weight and drops when the healthy leg lands. A severe hind-leg limp can make the head drop too, so the dog can look lame on a front leg — your veterinarian will confirm which leg is sore. When both hind legs hurt, the dog takes short steps behind and shifts its weight forward onto its front legs. A short video helps, because a limp does not always show at the clinic: film your dog walking towards you, away from you and past you. Some patterns are typical: a front-leg limp in a large young dog often comes from the elbow, a hind-leg limp in an adult dog from the cruciate ligament, and a small dog that skips for a few steps often has a slipping kneecap.

### Why is my puppy or young dog limping?

Do not wait for a young dog to “grow out of” a limp. Larger breeds can develop growth-related bone and joint diseases:
- Elbow dysplasia — developmental elbow problems that cause front-leg lameness and stiffness after rest, in breeds such as Labradors, Golden Retrievers, Bernese Mountain Dogs and Rottweilers; signs often start at 4–10 months of age, but some dogs are diagnosed only as adults.
- Osteochondrosis / osteochondritis dissecans (OCD) — faulty cartilage development in the shoulder, elbow, knee or hock, sometimes leaving a loose flap of cartilage in the joint.
- Hip dysplasia — a loose, malformed hip joint; some dogs bunny-hop, moving both hind legs together.
- Panosteitis — painful inflammation of the long bones in large-breed dogs aged about 6–16 months; the limp comes and goes, sometimes moves to another leg, and usually stops once the dog has finished growing.
In small breeds, typical causes are a slipping kneecap (patellar luxation) and Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease of the hip. Early diagnosis matters, because some of these conditions need surgery and the joint diseases lead to osteoarthritis. We also take official Kennel Club hip, elbow and spine X-rays (official examinations).
X-ray of the pelvis and hind legs of a dog with medial patellar luxation in both knees. The left kneecap (on the right of the image) has slipped out of its groove towards the inside of the knee (grade 3); the right knee is grade 2. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Why is my adult or older dog limping?

Common causes in adult dogs include paw injuries, sprains and strains after a slip or rough play, bite wounds, a slipping kneecap, fractures after an accident and, in a hind leg, cranial cruciate ligament disease — one of the most common causes of hind-leg lameness at this age. In older dogs, osteoarthritis becomes more common: an affected dog is slow to get up, stiff after rest and less keen to jump or play. A limp that does not go away should be X-rayed promptly — especially in a large- or giant-breed dog, or if there is a hard swelling on a leg bone — because a bone tumour is one possible cause. Not every limp starts in the leg: a slipped disc in the neck or back can press on the spinal cord or a nerve root and cause pain, lameness or weakness, particularly in breeds such as Dachshunds. If your dog suddenly cannot stand or walk, suddenly starts to drag its hind legs or knuckle over, or has sudden, severe back or neck pain, call a vet immediately, day or night. If it is wobbly but still walking, see a vet the same day.

### What happens at a lameness examination?

The veterinarian first asks which leg is affected, how the limp started, whether it is worse after rest or exercise, and whether there was an accident — bring any videos you have. They then watch your dog stand, walk and trot, compare both sides for muscle loss and joint swelling, and feel every bone and flex every joint, usually leaving the sore leg until last. Specific tests check, for example, whether the shin bone slides forward relative to the thigh bone — a sign of a torn cruciate ligament. This cruciate ligament test is done under deep sedation so that the leg muscles relax. A neurological check helps tell a spine or nerve problem from a joint problem. Lameness X-rays are taken under general anaesthesia so that the joints can be positioned correctly without pain (read more about anaesthesia safety). We have digital X-ray at the clinic (X-ray). For CT or other advanced imaging, we refer your dog elsewhere.

### What is a cruciate ligament rupture and how is it treated?

The cranial cruciate ligament stabilises the knee. In dogs it usually weakens gradually and often tears partially before it ruptures completely, and a partial tear almost always progresses to a full one. Typical signs are a hind-leg limp that starts suddenly or creeps up over weeks, stiffness after rest, and sitting with the leg stuck out to the side. An unstable knee can also damage the meniscus, the knee’s cartilage cushion, so do not wait. Surgery is usually recommended. At Saari Animal Clinic, veterinarian Pamela Kvarngård repairs cruciate ruptures using two methods. TTA suits active and large dogs. The lateral suture suits cats and small dogs, and often also medium-sized dogs and older, calmer large dogs. The choice depends on the individual dog. We check the menisci at every operation and treat any tear. We have performed knee surgery since 2017. Operations take place in a dedicated operating room used only for orthopaedic and other clean surgery. Recovery takes months of controlled, gradually increasing exercise. We always recommend physiotherapy after orthopaedic surgery: rehabilitation usually starts 1–2 weeks after the operation, and a visiting animal physiotherapist sees patients at our clinic.
Side-view X-ray of a dog’s left knee after TTA surgery: the tibial tuberosity has been moved forward, a titanium cage holds the osteotomy gap open, and a plate secured with a fork and screws fixes the tuberosity in place. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.

### How can I help my dog with osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis cannot be cured, but its pain can be managed — and it is not only a disease of old dogs. In a 2024 study of 123 dogs aged 8 months to 4 years, 40% had osteoarthritis on X-rays, most often in the elbow or hip. Among the dogs whose arthritic joints were also painful, owners had noticed signs in only about 3 in 10. International guidelines recommend combining:
- Weight control — keeping your dog lean takes load off the joints, improves mobility and can slow the disease.
- Regular, moderate exercise — walks of a steady length every day rather than sudden bursts of high-impact play; non-slip rugs and ramps help at home.
- Pain medication prescribed by a veterinarian — anti-inflammatory medicine, or a monthly injection that blocks a key pain signal in osteoarthritis (nerve growth factor); your veterinarian decides which option suits your dog.
- Rehabilitation — at our clinic this includes functional assessment, manual therapy and massage, electrotherapy and individual exercise programmes (rehabilitation).
- Acupuncture — given by veterinarian Assaf Wydra, who has advanced training in acupuncture for dogs and horses (acupuncture).
A joint diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids can also help.

### How much does a lameness examination cost?

At Saari Animal Clinic, a lameness examination costs €163. Deep sedation for the cruciate ligament test, if needed, is charged separately. A lameness examination with X-rays under general anaesthesia costs €273–323 (€323–453 for extensive examinations or large dogs). Prices for common orthopaedic operations:
- Cruciate ligament surgery, TTA €1,703 for dogs under 20 kg, €1,803 over 20 kg
- Cruciate ligament surgery, lateral suture €1,203 for dogs, €953 for cats
- Patellar luxation surgery €1,103–1,403 for dogs
- Femoral head ostectomy €1,203 for dogs
- Fracture surgery €1,203–2,003
- Toe amputation €593
The final cost depends on the findings and the treatment needed. Direct insurance billing is available for LähiTapiola, Agria and Pohjola customers. You will find all current prices in our price list.

### How do I book a lameness examination in Vaasa?

Book an examination if your adult dog’s limp is not clearly better after 24–48 hours of strict rest, gets worse or keeps coming back, or if a puppy or young dog limps. Call a vet immediately, day or night, if your dog has been hit by a car or had a bad fall, if you suspect an adder bite, or if it suddenly cannot stand or walk. See a vet the same day if your dog will not put any weight on the leg or is wobbly but still walking. At Saari Animal Clinic in Vaasa, we investigate lameness, take X-rays on site, operate on cruciate ligaments, kneecaps and fractures, and offer rehabilitation and acupuncture. Book by calling (06) 321 7300 or using our online booking. After hours, if your dog needs urgent care, call the Northern emergency area’s on-call vet on 0600 399 299.
