# Kidney Disease in Cats – Symptoms and Life Expectancy

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/kidney-disease-cats.html
Last updated: 2026-10-27

Pet Health
27.10.2026

## Chronic Kidney Disease in Cats — Symptoms, Stages, Treatment and Life Expectancy

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Chronic kidney disease (CKD), often called kidney failure, is one of the most common illnesses of older cats. Studies suggest that 30–40% or more of cats over 10 years old have some degree of it, although in most of them it is still at an early, mild stage. The kidneys lose function slowly and permanently, and because cats are good at hiding illness, the first signs are easy to miss. But kidney disease is not an immediate death sentence: with early diagnosis, a renal diet and the right treatment, many cats live for years with a good quality of life. This article explains which signs to watch for, how the disease is diagnosed and staged, how we treat it at Saari Animal Clinic, what to do when a kidney cat will not eat, and what to expect.
A regular check-up can reveal kidney disease before the cat shows any signs. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### What are the symptoms of kidney disease in cats?

The earliest signs are subtle. The cat drinks more and urinates more — the clumps in the litter tray get bigger or more numerous, or the tray needs changing more often. It may become fussier with food and slowly lose weight and muscle, especially along the spine and back legs. As the disease progresses, other signs appear: a dull, unkempt coat, vomiting, constipation, bad breath, mouth ulcers, lethargy and pale gums from anaemia. Many cats simply become quieter, hide more and groom less, which owners easily put down to old age. Low blood potassium, which is fairly common in kidney cats, can cause muscle weakness: a cat that holds its head bent down towards its chest needs to be seen promptly. High blood pressure caused by kidney disease can damage the eyes — wide pupils that do not shrink in light, bleeding inside the eye or sudden blindness need a vet the same day. In a US study of 569 cats, weight loss was already under way three years before diagnosis. In a large UK study, about one in three cats had no signs of illness recorded when kidney disease was diagnosed.

### What causes kidney disease in cats?

In most cats, chronic kidney disease is a slow scarring of the kidney tissue with age, and no single cause is found. Known contributors include an earlier episode of acute kidney injury, kidney infections, kidney and ureteral stones, high blood pressure and, less often, lymphoma of the kidneys. Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is an inherited condition in which fluid-filled cysts gradually replace kidney tissue. It occurs mainly in Persians and related breeds such as Exotic Shorthairs; a DNA test is available, and the cysts can be seen on ultrasound. Dental disease is linked with kidney disease in cats, although it has not been proven to cause it.

### Can a cat get kidney failure suddenly?

Yes. Acute kidney injury develops over hours or days, at any age, and is an emergency. In cats, the classic cause is lilies. All parts of true lilies (Lilium) and daylilies (Hemerocallis) are toxic to cats — the flowers, leaves, stems, pollen and even the water in the vase. Even a cat that only licks pollen off its fur can develop kidney failure. (Peace lilies and calla lilies are not true lilies: they can irritate the mouth but do not cause kidney failure.) Other causes include antifreeze (ethylene glycol), human painkillers such as ibuprofen, a stone blocking a ureter, a blocked urethra (a male cat that strains but passes little or no urine) and severe infections. If your cat may have chewed or licked any part of a lily, or come into contact with antifreeze, do not wait for symptoms. Call us at once, or the on-call vet on 0600 399 299 outside our opening hours, and bring the plant or a photo of it. Do not try to make your cat vomit at home: hydrogen peroxide, for example, can badly damage its stomach. With prompt treatment, most cats recover well; if treatment is delayed by 18 hours or more, kidney failure often develops and may be permanent or fatal. Once acute kidney injury has developed, the kidneys can often recover, but not always. In published studies of cats hospitalised for it — many of them severe cases on dialysis at specialist centres — about half died or were put to sleep before they could go home. Survivors can be left with lasting kidney damage.

### How is kidney disease diagnosed in cats?

Diagnosis is based on blood tests, a urine test and a blood pressure measurement. The blood test measures creatinine, urea, phosphorus, potassium and red blood cells, and at our clinic also SDMA — a kidney marker that usually rises earlier than creatinine. In a small study of research cats with kidney disease, SDMA rose before creatinine in 17 of 21 cats, on average about 17 months earlier. Creatinine also depends on muscle mass, so in a thin older cat it can make the kidneys look better than they are. The urine test shows whether the kidneys can still concentrate urine, whether protein is leaking into it (UPC ratio) and whether there are signs of infection. In cats, a urine specific gravity below 1.035 is a warning sign; wet food can lower it a little, but a low value still needs checking. When a urine culture is needed, we take the sample straight from the bladder with a fine needle. We measure blood pressure in the awake cat, in a calm room, using cuffs made for cats. An ultrasound scan shows the size and structure of the kidneys and checks for stones, blockage, cysts or tumours. One raised value is not a diagnosis: chronic kidney disease is confirmed and staged from tests taken on at least two occasions while the cat is stable and well hydrated.
Ultrasound image of the left kidney of a cat with chronic kidney disease. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.
The right kidney of the same cat on ultrasound: a cyst shows as a dark, fluid-filled area. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Why is the thyroid tested too?

An overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) is common in older cats and often occurs together with kidney disease. It increases blood flow through the kidneys and causes muscle loss, and both of these lower creatinine — so hyperthyroidism can hide kidney disease. That is why the thyroid hormone (T4) is tested in older cats with signs of kidney disease. It is also why kidney values are re-checked a few weeks (usually 2–4) after thyroid treatment starts: they often rise once the thyroid is under control. This rise usually does not mean the treatment harmed the kidneys; it reveals their true function. A thyroid level pushed too low, however, can itself reduce kidney function, so the dose is adjusted at follow-up checks. Treating the thyroid is still important, and the vet chooses the treatment and dose with the kidneys in mind.

### What are the IRIS stages of kidney disease in cats?

The International Renal Interest Society (IRIS) classifies chronic kidney disease into four stages based on blood creatinine and SDMA, measured on at least two occasions while the cat is stable and well hydrated. Stage 1 (creatinine below 140 µmol/l, SDMA below 18 µg/dl): kidney function is close to normal, but there are other signs of kidney disease. These include SDMA that stays slightly raised, dilute urine with no other cause, protein in the urine or abnormal kidneys on ultrasound. Stage 2 (creatinine 140–250 µmol/l, SDMA 18–25 µg/dl): mild disease; the cat often has no signs, or only increased thirst. Stage 3 (creatinine 251–440 µmol/l, SDMA 26–38 µg/dl): moderate disease; poor appetite, weight loss and vomiting are common. Stage 4 (creatinine above 440 µmol/l, SDMA above 38 µg/dl): severe disease, with a high risk of uraemic crises — nausea, refusal to eat, weakness. If SDMA stays higher than the creatinine value would suggest, for example in a thin cat with little muscle, the cat is staged and treated one stage higher. Each stage also has sub-stages for blood pressure and protein in the urine, which guide treatment and how often we re-check.

### How is kidney disease treated in cats?

Kidney disease cannot be cured, but its progress can often be slowed considerably, and the cat can feel well for a long time. The cornerstone is a renal diet (see below). If blood phosphorus stays high despite the diet, we add a phosphate binder, which is mixed into each meal. Fresh water must always be available. When needed, we give fluid therapy at the clinic, in our cat-only day ward: into a vein for cats that are dehydrated or in a uraemic crisis, or under the skin for some cats with advanced disease. Fluids are dosed carefully, because too much fluid can be harmful, especially in cats with heart disease. Other treatments depend on the stage and test results: medicine for high blood pressure and for protein in the urine (see below), potassium supplements when blood potassium is low, anti-nausea medicine, an appetite stimulant, and treatment for constipation, which is common in kidney cats. Anaemia is monitored at every check-up and treated case by case. Medicines that can harm the kidneys are avoided or used with care, and the doses of medicines cleared by the kidneys may need adjusting. Tell any vet who treats your cat that it has kidney disease. This matters for pain relief, because many older kidney cats also have painful arthritis, and their pain still needs treating. The product leaflets of anti-inflammatory pain medicines for cats advise against or restrict their use when kidney function is impaired. International feline guidelines, however, accept careful use in a cat with stable kidney disease, at the lowest effective dose and with regular check-ups; the vet weighs this for each cat. If a cat on such medicine stops eating, stop the medicine and contact us. Never give a cat human painkillers. The urine is checked for infection. An infection that reaches the kidneys can quickly worsen kidney function and is treated promptly, but bacteria in the urine of a cat with no signs of infection do not always need antibiotics. Dental disease is kept under control. We build an individual plan for each kidney cat and adjust it at every check-up.

### How are high blood pressure and protein in the urine treated?

High blood pressure is found in roughly one in five to two in five cats with kidney disease seen in general practice, and in up to two in three in some referral studies. It can damage the eyes, heart, brain and the kidneys themselves. Treatment is usually started when the systolic blood pressure stays at 160 mmHg or above on repeated measurements, or straight away if the eyes, brain or heart are already affected. Cats are typically given amlodipine or telmisartan; amlodipine is preferred when the pressure is very high or the eyes or brain are affected, because telmisartan has not been proven to work in those cats. If the urine protein:creatinine ratio (UPC) stays above 0.4, the cause is investigated. A medicine that blocks the renin–angiotensin system — telmisartan or benazepril — is then given together with the renal diet. Values between 0.2 and 0.4 are monitored closely, and treatment can be considered if they persist. All three medicines are licensed for cats: amlodipine for high blood pressure, benazepril for protein in the urine, and telmisartan for both. Unless the eyes or brain are in immediate danger, dehydration is corrected first, because in a dehydrated cat these medicines can make kidney function drop sharply. Blood pressure, urine protein and kidney values are re-checked after each change of dose.

### What should a cat with kidney disease eat?

A therapeutic renal diet is the treatment with the best evidence behind it. In two non-randomised studies, cats that ate a renal diet lived more than twice as long as cats that did not (a median of 633 versus 264 days in one of them). In a randomised trial in cats with stage 2–3 disease, none of the cats on the renal diet had a uraemic crisis, compared with about a quarter of those on ordinary food. Renal diets are low in phosphorus and contain moderate amounts of high-quality protein. They have added omega-3 fatty acids, potassium and B vitamins, and help counter the acid build-up that kidney disease can cause. Wet food is preferable because it also provides water — many kidney cats are mildly dehydrated all the time. Encourage drinking, too: several water bowls away from the food and the litter tray, a fountain, or a little extra water mixed into wet food. The vet will advise when to start the renal diet — usually from stage 2; it is easier to introduce while the appetite is still good. In some cats whose blood phosphorus is still normal, a renal diet can raise blood calcium, so calcium should be checked after the switch. Never start a renal diet while the cat is nauseous or in hospital: the cat can link the new food with feeling sick and refuse it afterwards. For the same reason, give tablets in a separate treat rather than hiding them in the renal food (phosphate binders are the exception: they are mixed into each meal as instructed). Switch foods gradually over several weeks, mixing the old food with the new. Never force a renal diet on a cat that refuses it: eating something is more important than eating the perfect food. We sell Royal Canin renal diets at the clinic, wet and dry, in several flavours and textures, so there is usually one your cat will accept. A home-made renal diet is possible only when it is formulated by a veterinary nutritionist — an unbalanced home diet can do more harm than good.

### My kidney cat won’t eat — what can I do?

Poor appetite is one of the most common problems in kidney cats, and it is often caused by nausea rather than fussiness. A cat that has eaten clearly less than usual for a couple of days, or nothing at all for a day, should be seen: going without food is dangerous for cats, and nausea can be treated. At home, offer small, fresh portions several times a day. Warm the wet food to body temperature to bring out its smell, and try different textures, such as pâté, chunks or dry food. Use a wide, shallow bowl in a quiet place. Anti-nausea medicine is often the first step, and an appetite stimulant can help. One appetite stimulant is licensed for cats that eat poorly and lose weight because of a long-term illness. It is an ointment rubbed once a day on the inner surface of the ear flap, which is easier than giving a tablet. Handling rules apply: wear disposable gloves, avoid contact with the cat for 12 hours after each application (so it is best given in the evening), and do not let the cat sleep in your bed during the treatment. Pregnant women, and women trying to conceive, should neither apply it nor touch the treated cat. A renal diet is the goal, but while a cat is eating poorly, any food it eats is better than none.

### How long can a cat live with kidney disease?

It depends mostly on the stage at diagnosis and on how well phosphorus, blood pressure, urine protein and appetite are managed. In a well-known study of 211 cats, those diagnosed at the upper end of stage 2 (creatinine above roughly 200 µmol/l) lived a median of about 3 years, and those in stage 3 about 2 years. Cats in stage 4 lived a median of about 3 months from diagnosis, but only about a month if they were still in stage 4 once dehydration had been corrected. Cats diagnosed earlier in stage 2 may do even better. Protein in the urine and high blood phosphorus are both linked with shorter survival, which is why we treat and monitor them. These figures are medians from studies of cats under veterinary care: half of the cats lived longer. They are not predictions for your cat — many cats outlive them with a renal diet they accept, a good appetite and regular check-ups.

### What does end-stage kidney failure look like in a cat?

In the final stage, the kidneys can no longer clear waste from the blood, and the cat becomes uraemic. It stops eating (and often drinking), vomits, loses weight quickly, is weak and sleeps most of the day, often in an unusual place. It may also have mouth ulcers, strong-smelling breath and, occasionally, tremors or seizures. A sudden worsening is not always the end, though: dehydration, a kidney infection or a stone blocking a ureter can be treated, so a kidney cat that suddenly gets worse should be seen promptly. Fluids, anti-nausea medicine and an appetite stimulant can bring back good days for a while. We help you judge quality of life honestly: is your cat still eating, grooming, moving about, seeking company and free of pain on most days? When the answer becomes no, euthanasia is the last kindness we can offer, and we talk about it with you openly and in good time.

### How often should a cat with kidney disease be checked?

After diagnosis, we usually re-check within 2–4 weeks to see how the diet and treatment are working. From then on, we check stable stage 2 cats every 3–6 months, stage 3 cats every 2–3 months and stage 4 cats every 1–2 months. A cat on blood pressure medicine should be checked at least every 3 months, even when stable. A check usually includes weight and muscle condition, blood pressure, a blood test (creatinine, SDMA, phosphorus, potassium, red blood cells) and a urine test. Between visits, weigh your cat at home every few weeks and note its appetite and drinking: a falling weight is often the first sign that the treatment needs adjusting. Frequent visits can be hard on cats, so we see them in a cat-only consulting room and never scruff them; for a very anxious cat, we can discuss calming medicine to give before the visit.
Your cat can come out of its carrier in its own time — we never pull it out. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Can kidney disease in cats be prevented or caught early?

Chronic kidney disease cannot be fully prevented, but it can be caught early — and treatment started in time, ideally by stage 2, gives the best chance of slowing it down. We recommend a yearly senior check-up from about 7 years of age. Ours includes the SDMA kidney test, and a urine test can be added. Look after your cat’s teeth, feed wet food if it drinks little, and never bring lilies into a home with a cat. If your cat is drinking more or losing weight, have it checked without delay. Even without signs, the yearly check-up matters: in a large UK study, about one in three cats had no signs of illness recorded when the disease was diagnosed.

### When should I bring my cat to the vet?

Book an appointment if your cat drinks or urinates more than before, has lost weight or appetite, vomits more often than usual or has bad breath. Contact us the same day if your cat suddenly goes blind, has eaten nothing for a day, is very weak or holds its head bent down. If your cat may have touched a lily or antifreeze, or a male cat strains in the litter tray but passes little or no urine, call at once. This is an emergency even before other signs appear. Blood and urine tests taken at the visit show whether the kidneys are involved; to confirm chronic kidney disease and its stage, we usually repeat them once the cat is stable. Saari Animal Clinic in Vaasa is an ISFM Cat Friendly Clinic and monitors kidney cats on an individual schedule. Call (06) 321 7300 or book online; outside our opening hours, call the on-call vet on 0600 399 299.
🐈 Cat vet in Vaasa – read more about our cat care

# Continuous Rate Infusion (CRI) | Saari Animal Clinic

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/pain-relief-infusion.html
Last updated: 2026-09-25

Anesthesia
25.9.2026

## Continuous Rate Infusion (CRI) — Steady Pain Management During Surgery

Veterinarian Pamela Kvarngård, Eläinklinikka Saari
Pain management is one of the most important parts of any surgery. At our clinic, a pain-relief infusion is a routine part of larger operations, such as dog spays and orthopedic surgery. It is known as a constant rate infusion (CRI), also called a continuous rate infusion. Rather than relying only on separate injections, a CRI delivers pain medication into a vein at a steady, precisely controlled rate, usually after a starting dose. We start the infusion before the first incision and continue it throughout the operation.

### Why Continuous Infusion?

When a pain medication is given as separate injections, its level in the blood rises after each dose and then falls. If it falls too low before the next dose, pain can break through, while high peaks can increase side effects. A continuous infusion keeps the level steadier, giving more even pain relief. The rate can also be adjusted as needed. In some studies of dogs undergoing major surgery, adding a ketamine infusion, alone or with lidocaine, reduced pain or the need for extra pain medication afterward.

### The Multimodal Approach

Each type of pain medication acts mainly at certain points along the pain pathway. Combining drugs that act at different points (multimodal pain relief) gives better pain control. Because each drug can then be used at a lower dose, the risk of side effects is also reduced. A pain-relief CRI is typically built around an opioid (a morphine-type pain medication), often combined with ketamine, lidocaine or dexmedetomidine. It is usually given alongside other pain relief, such as anti-inflammatory drugs or numbing local anesthetic blocks. The drugs are chosen to suit each patient and species.

### Less Anesthetic Gas Needed

Pain-relief infusions can also reduce the amount of anesthetic gas needed. In a laboratory study, six dogs were anesthetized with isoflurane — the gas we use. Low-dose infusions of morphine, lidocaine and ketamine, alone or combined, reduced the amount of isoflurane needed by about 25–50% without lowering blood pressure. Pain guidelines note that this effect of lidocaine may help dogs with low blood pressure who would otherwise need a lot of gas. In a similar study in cats, lidocaine also reduced the amount of gas needed, but the cats’ hearts pumped less blood than under equally deep anesthesia with gas alone. Lidocaine infusions are therefore used in cats only with caution.

### Use at Our Clinic

We routinely use a multimodal pain-relief CRI in dog spays, tumor and mammary surgery, abdominal surgery and orthopedic surgery, such as cruciate ligament and fracture repair. When needed, the infusion continues after surgery. Castrations and cat spays are painful too, but for these operations we provide pain relief in other ways.

### What Is Pain “Wind-Up”?

When pain signals keep arriving, nerve cells in the spinal cord can respond more and more strongly — this is called wind-up. A related, longer-lasting change is central sensitization: the nervous system amplifies pain so that even light touch can hurt. Because pain that has already set in is harder to treat, pain guidelines recommend giving pain relief before, during and after surgery. Ketamine, often part of a CRI, blocks NMDA receptors — nerve-cell receptors that play a key role in this amplification. However, more research is needed on its use around surgery. Good pain control reduces the risk of sensitization but cannot rule it out.

### Safety

Using several drugs at lower doses helps reduce side effects, but any drug can still cause them. CRI drugs can, for example, lower blood pressure or heart rate, or cause a restless recovery. Every patient is monitored throughout anesthesia, and the anesthetist adjusts the infusion rate according to what the monitoring shows. Feel free to ask us how your pet’s pain will be managed.
An anaesthetised patient is monitored in the operating room throughout the procedure. In the background, an infusion pump and a patient monitor on the drip stand. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

# Diarrhoea in Dogs and Cats | Saari Animal Clinic

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/diarrhoea.html
Last updated: 2026-09-25

Health
25.9.2026

## Diarrhoea in Dogs and Cats — Causes, Home Care and When to Contact the Clinic

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Diarrhoea is one of the most common reasons for a veterinary visit. Most cases are mild and settle within a few days — but diarrhoea can also be a sign of serious illness. Here is what causes it, how to care for your pet at home and when to contact the clinic.

### Most Common Causes

In dogs, the most common cause is eating something unsuitable, such as rubbish or table scraps, or changing food too quickly. In cats, a sudden change of diet is a common trigger. Other causes include intestinal parasites (such as Giardia, roundworms and coccidia), stress, food allergy or intolerance, toxins and swallowed foreign objects. Bacterial and viral infections are also possible — the most serious being parvovirus in unvaccinated puppies and panleukopenia (feline parvovirus) in unvaccinated kittens. Diarrhoea that lasts longer than about three weeks or keeps coming back is called chronic and always needs investigating.

### Home Care

If your adult pet is otherwise bright, eating and drinking normally, and the diarrhoea is not bloody, you can try home care for 24–48 hours. Do not starve your pet: fasting is no longer recommended — even dogs with severe intestinal infection recovered faster when fed early. Cats especially must keep eating: after just a few days of eating little or nothing, a cat — particularly an overweight one — can develop dangerous fatty liver (hepatic lipidosis). Offer a bland, low-fat, easily digestible diet in small portions 4–6 times a day. The clinic sells Royal Canin Gastro Intestinal diets for dogs and cats; for a few days, boiled skinless, boneless chicken with boiled rice (about one part chicken to two parts rice) also works, but it is not a complete long-term diet. Always provide fresh water. Once the stool is normal, continue the bland diet for a few days, then return gradually to the usual food over about a week. Wash your hands after cleaning up: some causes, such as Campylobacter and Salmonella bacteria, can spread to people. Supervise children’s handwashing.

### Probiotics and Medicines

A veterinary probiotic may help — for cats, the clinic sells FortiFlora — although the evidence is modest. Never give human medicines without veterinary advice. Loperamide (Imodium) can cause serious neurological poisoning in dogs carrying the MDR1 gene mutation — common in Collies, Australian Shepherds and Shelties, and also found in other breeds and crosses. Products containing bismuth subsalicylate (such as Pepto-Bismol, sold abroad) can poison cats. In dogs, international guidelines advise against antibiotics for acute diarrhoea — even when it contains blood — unless the dog is severely ill.

### When to Contact the Veterinarian

Contact the clinic the same day if: the diarrhoea contains blood (bright red, or black and tarry); your pet vomits repeatedly or cannot keep water down; your pet is lethargic or weak, or its belly seems painful; you see signs of dehydration (dry, tacky gums, sunken eyes, or skin that is slow to fall back when gently lifted); your pet may have eaten something poisonous or a foreign object; or your cat has not eaten for more than a day. A male cat straining in the litter box may have a urinary blockage — an emergency. Puppies and kittens — especially unvaccinated ones — need prompt assessment: they dehydrate quickly, and parvovirus can be life-threatening. Elderly pets, small breeds and chronically ill animals also dehydrate faster. If there is no improvement after 48 hours of home care, or the diarrhoea recurs, book an examination. Tip: a photo of the stool helps the veterinarian.

### Prevention

Change food gradually over 7–10 days. Avoid table scraps, bones and access to rubbish. Deworm according to your pet’s risk — a faecal sample helps show whether treatment is needed. Pharmacies sell dewormers without a prescription, but they do not treat every cause of diarrhoea — Giardia and coccidia, for example, need a diagnosis and a specific treatment. Keep vaccinations up to date. Reduce stress during changes; pheromone products (such as Feliway for cats) may help some animals, though the evidence is limited.

### Contact Us

If you are unsure, call us on (06) 321 7300 or email info@saarivet.fi — you can attach photos. We will advise whether a visit is needed.

# Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) in Dogs | Saari Animal Clinic

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/patent-ductus-arteriosus-pda.html
Last updated: 2026-09-27

Cardiology
27.9.2026

## Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) in Dogs — A Congenital Heart Defect That Can Usually Be Cured

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is one of the most common congenital heart defects in dogs. The ductus is a blood vessel that connects the aorta and the pulmonary artery before birth; it should close soon afterward. If it stays open, it overloads the heart, and most untreated dogs develop heart failure within their first year or two. When PDA is found early and closed, it is usually cured.

### What Is PDA?

Before birth the lungs are not yet working, and the ductus lets blood bypass them. After birth the lungs fill with air, oxygen levels rise and the ductus constricts. In dogs it normally closes within the first week of life. In PDA it stays open. Blood then flows continuously from the aorta into the pulmonary artery, through the lungs and back to the left side of the heart, which becomes overloaded and enlarges. The larger the ductus, the heavier the load.

### Predisposed Breeds

PDA has a genetic basis, and about three out of four affected dogs are female. It is most common in small breeds such as the Bichon Frise, Chihuahua, Maltese, Pomeranian, Poodle, Yorkshire Terrier and Shetland Sheepdog, but larger breeds such as the German Shepherd can also be affected. Dogs with PDA should not be bred, even after successful treatment. Their parents, siblings and offspring should also have their hearts checked. PDA occurs in cats as well, but less often.

### Signs — What Owners May Notice

Most puppies with PDA seem healthy when the defect is found, and in some dogs it is not detected until adulthood. It is usually discovered at a routine puppy visit, when the vet hears a continuous “machinery murmur.” Sometimes you can feel a buzzing vibration on the left side of the chest. Some puppies are lethargic, tire quickly during play, breathe fast or cough. Fast or labored breathing at rest can be a sign of fluid in the lungs (heart failure) and needs urgent veterinary care.

### Reversed PDA — An Important Exception

In a small minority of dogs, a large PDA causes severe high blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension), and blood flows the “wrong” way, from the pulmonary artery into the aorta. The typical murmur then disappears. The dog may tire easily or collapse during exercise, with weakness in the hind legs. The vulva or prepuce may look bluish while the gums stay pink. Oxygen-poor blood reaches the kidneys, which then make the body produce too many red blood cells (polycythemia). The ductus must not be closed in these dogs, because closure can cause life-threatening right-sided heart failure. Treatment includes medication such as sildenafil and keeping the red blood cell count down, either by periodically removing blood or with the drug hydroxyurea. The long-term outlook is guarded to poor, although survival varies widely and some dogs live for years.

### Treatment

Typical (left-to-right) PDA is treated by closing the ductus. In surgery, the chest is opened and the ductus is tied off. In catheter closure, a device, most often the Amplatz Canine Duct Occluder (ACDO), is passed through a blood vessel, usually in the groin, and seals the ductus from inside. This method is less invasive, but the dog must be big enough for the device, so very small dogs often have surgery. Both methods succeed in most dogs. Deaths are uncommon: in a study of 456 dogs, 2.6% died within three days of the procedure, and in a 2025 study of 200 dogs whose ductus was closed with the ACDO, 0.5% died. The risk is higher if the heart is already markedly enlarged. Medication can stabilize a dog in heart failure before closure but does not cure PDA. Closure is best done soon after diagnosis, ideally before any signs of heart failure.

### Diagnosis at Our Clinic

At Eläinklinikka Saari, every puppy’s heart is listened to at its first visit. If we hear a murmur, our veterinarian Leena Sandström can examine the heart with ultrasound (echocardiography) at the clinic. The examination confirms PDA, shows how much strain it causes and checks for other heart defects. We do not close PDAs ourselves: if closure is needed, we refer your dog to a veterinary hospital that performs the procedure.

### Prognosis

When the ductus is closed before heart failure develops, the prognosis is excellent and most dogs live a normal lifespan. The heart starts to shrink within a day of closure and usually returns to, or close to, normal size over the following months. A follow-up ultrasound checks that the ductus has sealed completely. Without closure the outlook is poor. In a US study of 520 dogs, the estimated median survival of those with no other heart defect was about 12 years with closure and about 2 years without. Few dogs in the study went untreated, so these figures are rough estimates.

### The Most Important Message for Owners

Every puppy’s heart should be listened to at its first veterinary visit. If a murmur is heard, a cardiac ultrasound should be done without delay. PDA can usually be cured — as long as it is found in time. Owners and breeders of predisposed breeds should be especially vigilant.

# Tooth Brushing for Dogs and Cats – How to Get Started

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/tooth-brushing.html
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Dental
27.9.2026

## Tooth Brushing — The Best Thing You Can Do for Your Pet’s Teeth

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Gum (periodontal) disease is one of the most common health problems in dogs and cats. Thorough examinations under anesthesia find at least early gum disease in most adult pets, often by two to three years of age. It causes pain and infection and has been linked to heart, kidney and liver disease. Daily tooth brushing is the most effective way to prevent it at home — and many pets learn to accept it.

### Why Daily?

Plaque — a sticky film of bacteria — re-forms within a day of cleaning and within a few days starts hardening into tartar, which brushing cannot remove. Plaque at and just below the gumline is what inflames the gums; daily brushing keeps ahead of it. In studies in dogs, more frequent brushing worked better: in one, brushing every other day was not enough to keep the gums healthy, and in another, gum inflammation was back after four weeks without brushing.

### How to Brush Your Pet’s Teeth

Always use pet toothpaste. Pets swallow the paste, and human toothpastes usually contain foaming agents and fluoride that can upset the stomach; some also contain xylitol, which is poisonous to dogs. Use a soft brush sized to the mouth — a children’s toothbrush often fits smaller dogs, and an infant brush often suits cats and toy breeds. A finger brush helps while your pet is learning. Lift the lip, angle the bristles at about 45 degrees toward the gumline and brush in small circles. Brush the outer surfaces first, with the mouth closed, sliding the brush inside the cheek to reach the back teeth. If your pet allows, brush the inner surfaces too. It all takes less than 2 minutes.

### Getting Your Pet Used to Brushing

Go at your pet’s pace; the week-by-week steps are only a guide. Week 1: touch the lips and teeth with your finger. Week 2: let your pet lick toothpaste from your finger, then rub a little on the front teeth. Week 3: introduce the brush and brush a few teeth, then gradually more. Always reward your pet afterward. Never force the mouth open; keep sessions short and positive, and stop if your pet becomes stressed or tries to bite. Start handling practice while your pet is a puppy or kitten, and begin daily brushing once the adult teeth are in (at about 6–7 months). Adult pets can learn too. If your pet already has tartar, red gums or bad breath, book a dental check first.

### Signs of Dental Disease

Watch for bad breath (it is not normal); red, swollen or bleeding gums; and visible tartar. Other signs include dropping food, chewing on one side only, drooling, pawing at the mouth, facial swelling, reluctance to have the head touched, behavioral changes and weight loss. Animals hide pain: many keep eating even when the mouth hurts badly, so a normal appetite does not mean a healthy mouth. After treatment, pets may become livelier, sleep better or even become friendlier.
Periodontal disease in an adult dog: heavy tartar on the premolars and molars, and the gums are inflamed and receding in places. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Professional Dental Cleaning

Even with good home care, many pets, especially older ones, need professional cleaning under general anesthesia from time to time. We recommend a dental check at least once a year; a quick check without anesthesia helps us assess whether treatment is needed. Under anesthesia we clean below the gumline, where gum disease is active. We also examine every tooth and usually take dental X-rays: in studies of pets referred for dental treatment, X-rays of normal-looking teeth revealed important problems in more than one in four dogs and about four in ten cats. General anesthesia is essential: so-called “anesthesia-free dental cleaning” is purely cosmetic, cannot treat disease below the gumline and gives a false sense of security.

### What Else Helps?

Dental chews and diets can help, but less than brushing. Look for the VOHC (Veterinary Oral Health Council) seal, awarded when trials show a product slows the buildup of plaque or tartar. Choose the right size of chew and supervise chewing; avoid very hard chews such as antlers, hooves or nylon bones, which can break teeth. We sell pet toothpaste and soft toothbrushes for dogs and cats.

### #BrushChamp — Do You Brush Every Day?

At Eläinklinikka Saari we value owners who commit to daily tooth brushing. If you brush your pet’s teeth every day, let us know — dedicated brushers receive the #BrushChamp medal! Contact us at the clinic or by email: info@saarivet.fi.

# Grain-Free Food for Dogs and Cats | Saari Animal Clinic

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/grain-free-food.html
Last updated: 2026-09-27

Health
27.9.2026

## Grain-Free Food for Dogs and Cats — Is It Necessary or Harmful?

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Grain-free pet food became a major trend, marketed as more “natural”. But in July 2018 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced an investigation into heart disease (DCM) in dogs eating certain foods, many of them grain-free. Here we review what the research shows — and what we recommend.

### The FDA Investigation and Heart Disease

In dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), usually a hereditary disease of large breeds, the heart muscle weakens and the heart enlarges. The FDA’s 2019 summary of 515 canine reports from January 2014 to April 2019 included many breeds not known to be predisposed, most often Golden Retrievers, mixed breeds and Labradors. Over 90% of the products named were grain-free and 93% contained peas and/or lentils — but voluntary reports do not show how common the disease is. The FDA notes that most of the reported foods, including some grain-containing ones, had pulses (peas, lentils, chickpeas, beans) high in the ingredient list, and that pulses have long been used in pet foods “with no evidence to indicate they are inherently dangerous”. The agency has not established a causal link, and in December 2022 it said it would publish no further updates until there is meaningful new scientific information.
Side-view chest X-ray of a dog with a heart change resembling dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM phenotype): the heart shadow is enlarged. An X-ray does not show the cause – that is investigated with a heart ultrasound. Image: Saari Animal Clinic.

### What Controlled Feeding Trials Show

Feeding trials have given mixed results. In 28 Siberian Huskies fed diets containing 0–45% whole pulses for 20 weeks, heart ultrasound findings and heart-related blood tests were unchanged. In an 18-month randomised trial of 60 dogs on four foods, the heart-related blood tests stayed normal and no dog developed DCM, but dogs on a grain-containing food rich in peas and pea fibre ended the trial with slightly weaker, though still normal, heart contraction than those on pea-free foods. The authors suggested valve disease as one possible explanation; in a letter, over 100 veterinary cardiologists disagreed, linking the change to the pea ingredients rather than to a lack of grain. In eight Beagles, four weeks on an experimental food containing 58% pea flour (of a type not sold commercially) caused mild, symptom-free changes resembling early DCM; a lentil-based food did not. The trials are small, and most are far shorter than the year or more for which affected dogs have typically eaten such food.

### Studies of Dogs Eating Their Usual Food

Such studies show associations, not causation. Among 188 healthy dogs, extra heartbeats from the heart’s lower chambers were more common in those whose food listed peas, lentils or potatoes among the first ten ingredients (10% vs 2%). Dogs on these foods, or on grain-free foods, also had higher troponin, a blood marker possibly signalling low-level heart muscle damage. In a separate study, Irish Wolfhounds on high-pulse food likewise had more extra beats (6 of 35 vs 1 of 62). Occasional extra beats also occur in healthy dogs, and heart ultrasound showed no differences in either study. In another 46 healthy dogs, however, those on pulse-rich foods had weaker heart contraction and a larger main pumping chamber. Among 60 dogs with DCM, the 51 that had eaten such foods improved slightly more after a diet change and treatment than the 9 that had not. Yet in the US Dog Aging Project (over 47,000 dogs), owner-reported grain-free feeding was not linked to new heart diagnoses over two years. These diagnoses were mostly murmurs rather than DCM specifically, and pulses were not analysed. A link is neither confirmed nor ruled out; research increasingly focuses on pulses rather than on a lack of grain.

### Does My Pet Need Grain-Free Food?

Probably not. Science does not support claims that grains are mere “fillers” or the main cause of food allergies. As farming spread, most dogs gained extra copies of the starch-digesting AMY2B gene — on average about five times as many as wolves — though some Arctic breeds, such as the Siberian Husky, have few (Arendt et al., 2016). In one study, dogs digested over 99% of the starch in cooked cereal-based diets (Murray et al., 1999). Grains are also less common allergens than the main animal proteins, though wheat is not a rare one: of 297 dogs with confirmed food allergy, 34% reacted to beef, 17% to dairy, 15% to chicken, 13% to wheat, 4% to corn and 2% to rice — figures that may partly reflect what dogs have usually eaten (Mueller et al., 2016).

### What About Cats?

Cats are obligate carnivores: they need plenty of animal protein and must get taurine from food, as a lack of it weakens the heart muscle (Pion et al., 1987). Grain-free cat foods often replace grains with potatoes, peas or tapioca. In one comparison of dry foods, grain-free ones averaged about a quarter less carbohydrate than grain-containing ones, but with wide overlap, so grain-free does not necessarily mean low-carbohydrate (Prantil et al., 2018). Cats also digest cooked starch well: over 93% of it in all six dry foods tested, including pea- and lentil-based ones (de-Oliveira et al., 2008). By July 2020, over 20 cats with DCM had been reported to the FDA, compared with over 1,100 dogs. What matters most is adequate animal protein and taurine — not whether the food is grain-free.

### Veterinary Recommendation

Grain-free food has no proven benefit for healthy dogs or cats, so choose it only for a medical reason. The FDA says it has no definitive information that these foods are inherently unsafe. Tufts University veterinary nutritionists nevertheless regard pulses among the first ten ingredients as a possible risk for some dogs and, for dogs with DCM, recommend a food without pulses or potatoes alongside treatment. If your dog’s food lists pulses among its first ten ingredients, talk to your vet, especially if your dog has a heart murmur or belongs to a breed prone to heart disease. The World Small Animal Veterinary Association (WSAVA) suggests asking manufacturers who formulates the food — ideally a qualified nutritionist — and what research they have done. Food allergy is diagnosed with an elimination diet of at least eight weeks followed by a re-challenge, not by switching foods at random. Tiring easily, coughing, breathing difficulty or fainting always need investigating, whatever the food. DCM can also progress without signs; we can listen to the heart and, if needed, examine it with ultrasound. Eläinklinikka Saari sells pet food; we mention this for transparency.

# PerioVive Gel for Periodontal Disease in Dogs and Cats

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/periovive.html
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Dental
27.9.2026

## PerioVive — Hyaluronic Acid Gel as an Add-On in Periodontal Disease Treatment

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Periodontal disease is one of the most common diseases in dogs and cats: UK veterinary practices diagnose it in about 12.5% of dogs and 15% of cats in a given year, and detailed examinations under anesthesia find it in 44–100% of dogs. Left untreated, it can destroy the tissues that hold the teeth, causing bone loss and eventually tooth loss. PerioVive is a hyaluronic acid gel used as an add-on during dental procedures — not a stand-alone treatment.
Periodontal disease in an adult dog: heavy tartar on the premolars and molars, and the gums are inflamed and receding in places. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### What is PerioVive?

PerioVive is a gel containing 0.8% hyaluronic acid (HA), made for veterinary dental procedures. HA occurs naturally in the gums and in the tissues that anchor the teeth, and it takes part in inflammation and wound healing. At the end of the procedure, the gel is placed into cleaned pockets, extraction sockets or surgical sites. PerioVive is sold as a veterinary medical device, not as an authorized medicine, so no medicines authority has assessed its efficacy.

### How Does It Work?

Laboratory and animal studies suggest that hyaluronic acid can dampen inflammation, help stabilize the blood clot in a wound, slow the growth of some bacteria and support the cells that rebuild gum, bone and the tooth’s attachment. Whether these effects improve healing in pets with naturally occurring periodontal disease is not yet known.

### Scientific Evidence

The best evidence comes from studies in humans. In a meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials (Eliezer et al. 2019), adding HA reduced pocket depth by about 0.4 mm more after non-surgical treatment and 0.9 mm more after surgery (two trials), but results varied widely and the risk of bias was high. A 2026 meta-analysis (Rotundo et al.) also found small gains after non-surgical treatment, but they were not confirmed in trials at low risk of bias. Small studies in laboratory dogs with experimentally created defects have generally found better healing with HA on microscopic examination. In one (Tella et al. 2023; four dogs, assessed at three months), new bone filled about 89% of the defect height when HA gel was added to surgical root cleaning, versus 39% with cleaning alone. In another (Shirakata et al. 2022; six dogs), HA produced more new tissue anchoring the root, but not significantly more bone. None used PerioVive; Tella et al. used a different 0.8% HA gel. No side effects were reported in these dog studies.

### What Are the Limitations?

To our knowledge, no controlled study has been published on HA gels in pet dogs or cats with naturally occurring periodontal disease, or on PerioVive itself; data from cats are especially scarce. HA gel is an add-on, never a replacement for the basics: cleaning above and below the gumline under anesthesia, full-mouth dental X-rays, extraction of teeth that cannot be saved and daily tooth brushing. Without home care, plaque returns within a day and cleaned pockets can be reinfected within two weeks.

### When is PerioVive Used?

PerioVive can be used in cleaned pockets around teeth worth keeping, in extraction sockets and in gum surgery. It is applied once, under the same anesthesia as the dental procedure, so no extra visit is needed. It has not been shown to save a loose tooth or one that has lost most of its supporting bone — such teeth usually need to be extracted.

### PerioVive Treatment at Our Clinic

At Eläinklinikka Saari we use PerioVive in dogs and cats as an add-on during dental procedures under general anesthesia — usually with full-mouth dental X-rays and scaling, and in surgery such as removing a dental cyst. The gel is charged by the amount used; a typical treatment needs only a fraction of a milliliter. Ask us at your pet’s next visit or call (06) 321 7300 — we will assess whether your pet might benefit.

### Sources

- O’Neill D.G. ym. (2023): Periodontal disease in cats under primary veterinary care in the UK: frequency and risk factors. Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery 25(3):1098612X231158154. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/PMC10812011

# Why Choosing an Independent Veterinary Clinic Matters

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/independent-clinic.html
Last updated: 2026-09-27

Clinic
27.9.2026

## Why Choosing an Independent Veterinary Clinic Matters

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
In a 2024 report, the Finnish Competition and Consumer Authority (KKV) found that the Finnish market for small-animal veterinary care had concentrated heavily through acquisitions over the previous ten years and was led by two chains owned by foreign private equity investors — Evidensia and Vireä. Measured by 2023 revenue, Evidensia had 40–50% of the private small-animal market nationally and Vireä 10–20% (KKV gives ranges to protect business secrets). Eläinklinikka Saari is the only family-owned small-animal clinic in Vaasa, and we want to explain why that matters to us.

### Chains in Finland

Evidensia belongs to the international IVC Evidensia group, whose largest shareholder is the Swedish private equity firm EQT. In a deal announced in February 2021, the US investment firm Silver Lake took a minority stake and Nestlé increased its own. The deal valued the whole group, debt included, at about €12.3 billion. When KKV carried out its study in 2024, Evidensia had 47 locations in mainland Finland. Vireä, part of the Vetopia group, had 13 locations offering small-animal care; KKV named the Danish private equity firm Axcel as Vireä’s largest owner. Evidensia is particularly strong in hospital care: by KKV’s definition, 13 of the 18 private small-animal hospitals in mainland Finland belonged to Evidensia, and however hospitals were defined, its national share of that market was over 70%.

### Impact on Prices

KKV’s November 2024 report examined prices after Evidensia bought Omaeläinklinikka, then the second-largest chain, in 2021. Between September 2021 and April 2024, the list prices published by Evidensia’s clinics and the former Omaeläinklinikka clinics rose by 28% on average, while consumer prices rose by 15% and Statistics Finland’s price index for veterinary services by 13%. KKV concluded that the results indicate the acquisition led to a significant price increase. The 28% figure is an average across individual procedures, not the change in the cost of an average visit. Separately, household spending on veterinary and other pet services more than doubled in ten years, from €235 million in 2014 to €501 million in 2024 (Statistics Finland, preliminary figure for 2024). That is total spending, not prices: the number of dogs rose from about 450,000 in 2012 to an estimated 800,000-plus in 2023. KKV links rising costs to general cost increases and advances in veterinary medicine, as well as to market concentration and a lack of competition.

### What Does Chain Ownership Mean for Care?

In our view, who owns a clinic shapes its priorities. In a report of 14 July 2023 on the concentration of the Finnish veterinary market, Yle quoted Mikko Turku, then chair of the Finnish Veterinary Association. He saw it as a challenge that large operators can strongly influence pricing and what kinds of treatment are given: when an instruction comes from the top, an individual vet may not be able to practise as independently as they should. This is his view as reported by Yle, not a finding of a regulator.

### International Examples

The UK has seen similar consolidation. In its final report of 24 March 2026, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) found that six large groups own over 60% of UK vet practices, wholly or in part; in 2013, large groups owned about 10%. Between 2016 and 2023, average prices across the sector rose by 63%, against general inflation of 32%. The CMA also found that from January 2023 to July 2024, average prices at practices owned by five of the six groups (IVC Evidensia among them) were together 18.3% higher than at independent practices — a comparison that does not adjust for possible differences in quality or costs. In Sweden and Norway, a peer-reviewed study of 771 clinics by Egenvall and colleagues found that during 2023 the median price increase (in euros) was 15% at Evidensia clinics, 8% at clinics of the AniCura chain and 6% at independent clinics. As possible reasons for price differences between clinics, the authors list investment in equipment or staffing, spending on staff training, and different demands for profit.

### Eläinklinikka Saari — A Conscious Choice

We have received several offers from chains wanting to buy our clinic, and we have chosen to remain independent. The clinic is owned by two veterinarians, Assaf Wydra and Pamela Kvarngård, not by outside investors. We set our own prices, and our profits stay in Vaasa. We are a small team, so our vets get to know you and your pet. When you choose an independent clinic, you also support local entrepreneurship and competition in a market that KKV expects to become further concentrated.
The Saari Animal Clinic team outside the clinic in Vaasa. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Sources

- Jankari A. ym. (2024): Selvitys pieneläinlääkäripalveluiden kilpailutilanteesta ja markkinoiden keskittymisen vaikutuksista. Kilpailu- ja kuluttajaviraston katsauksia 6/2024, 5.11.2024. kkv.fi
- Tilastokeskus (2026): Kotitalouksien kulutusmenot (COICOP2018), vuosittain, 1990–2025*, taulukko 15ag; luokka 09.4.5 Eläinlääkintäpalvelut ja muut lemmikkieläinpalvelut. Päivitetty 18.9.2026. pxdata.stat.fi
- EQT (2021): IVC Evidensia expands partnership to drive next phase of accelerating growth. Tiedote, 9.2.2021. eqtgroup.com
- Laakso L.-K. (2023): Työntekijät kertovat lähes monopoliaseman hankkineen Evidensian ongelmista: ”En enää kehtaa kertoa, missä olen töissä”. Yle, 14.7.2023. yle.fi

# Food Allergies in Dogs and Cats | Saari Animal Clinic

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/food-allergies.html
Last updated: 2026-09-27

Pet Health
27.9.2026

## Food Allergies in Dogs and Cats — Symptoms, Diagnosis and Elimination Diet

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Food allergy is one cause of itching in dogs and cats. In studies, it is found in roughly 15–20% of itchy pets — less often than environmental allergy (atopy). Many owners suspect grains, but the most common culprits in dogs are animal proteins such as beef, dairy products and chicken. Food allergy can only be diagnosed with an elimination diet and a food challenge, and we can help you with both.

### Symptoms

The most common signs of food allergy are itching, paw licking and recurring ear and skin infections. Some pets also have vomiting, diarrhoea or more frequent bowel movements than normal. Cats often scratch their head, face and neck, and many overgroom until bald patches appear. Food allergy is usually not seasonal, but environmental allergy is often year-round too, so year-round itching alone does not prove that food is to blame. In dogs, food allergy is more likely if the itching comes with digestive signs. It can start at any age; in almost 40% of food-allergic dogs, the signs had begun by the age of one.
Otitis externa in a dog: the skin around the opening of the ear canal is red and scaly, with yellow-brown discharge in the hair. Recurrent ear infections can be a sign of food allergy, but they also have many other causes. Photo: Saari Animal Clinic.

### Most Common Allergens

In dogs whose food allergy was confirmed with a food challenge, the most common triggers were beef (34% of dogs), dairy products (17%), chicken (15%) and wheat (13%). Less common triggers were soy (6%), lamb (5%) and corn (4%). Some dogs reacted to several foods. Cats have been studied less, but beef, fish and dairy products were their most common triggers. Wheat is the only grain among the common triggers. The figures may reflect what pets have most often been fed. “Grain-free” food is not the solution, because it often still contains the most common allergens, such as beef or chicken.

### Elimination Diet — The Only Reliable Diagnostic Method

Blood tests for food allergy are not reliable: the same sample tested repeatedly gave inconsistent results, and accuracy varied greatly in dogs and was low in cats. Hair and saliva tests are not reliable either. The reliable method is an elimination diet: for at least 8 weeks, your pet eats nothing but a veterinary elimination diet, while parasites and skin infections are ruled out or treated. The diet is either a hydrolysed-protein food, in which the proteins are broken down into fragments so small that the immune system usually no longer recognises them, or a food based on a protein your pet has never eaten before. In studies, more than 90% of food-allergic dogs and cats had improved within 8 weeks.

### Elimination Diet Rules

The elimination diet must be absolutely strict: your pet may have only the elimination food and water. No treats, human food, rawhide or chew bones, flavoured toothpaste, pills hidden in food, or flavoured medicines such as chewable worming or flea and tick tablets. Where possible, medicines are switched to unflavoured forms, such as spot-on parasite treatments. Make sure the whole family follows the rules and that your pet cannot scavenge, hunt or eat other pets’ food. Shop-bought “limited-ingredient” or “novel protein” foods are not suitable: in studies, 33–83% of limited-ingredient and novel-protein foods, including some veterinary ones, contained ingredients not listed on the label. Hydrolysed diets have fared better. That is why we use veterinary elimination diets and follow your pet’s response closely. If the itching does not settle, a second trial with a different diet may be needed.

### Challenge Phase and Long-Term Management

If the signs improve on the elimination diet, the diagnosis is confirmed by reintroducing the old food. In studies, about half of food-allergic dogs flared up within five days and about 90% within two weeks; cats reacted faster — half within four days and about 90% within a week. Continue the challenge for a full two weeks before concluding that food is not the cause. If the signs return, your pet goes back on the elimination diet until they settle. Individual proteins can then be tested one at a time to show which are safe and which must be avoided. Food allergy cannot be cured, but avoiding the trigger foods usually keeps the signs away without medication. Some pets also have environmental allergy and may still need other treatment.

### Food Allergy Investigations at Our Clinic

At Eläinklinikka Saari, we help you investigate and manage food allergy. We plan an individual elimination diet for your pet, treat secondary skin and ear infections at the same time, and follow progress throughout the process. We also sell elimination diets at the clinic and can help you choose the right one.

### Sources

# Hyperthyroidism in Cats | Saari Animal Clinic

URL: https://elainklinikkasaari.fi/en/articles/hyperthyroidism.html
Last updated: 2026-10-30

Cat Health
30.10.2026

## Hyperthyroidism in Cats — Symptoms, Diagnosis and Treatment

Veterinarian Assaf Wydra, Eläinklinikka Saari
Hyperthyroidism is the most common hormonal disease in older cats. Depending on the study, it affects up to about one in ten cats over 10 years of age. The overactive thyroid gland produces too much thyroid hormone (T4), which speeds up the metabolism and strains many organs, especially the heart and kidneys. Left untreated, the disease leads to serious complications. With treatment and regular check-ups, the outlook is usually good, although kidney disease found alongside it can affect the long-term prognosis.

### Symptoms

The most common signs are weight loss despite a good or increased appetite, increased drinking and urination, vomiting, diarrhea, hyperactivity or restlessness, increased vocalization, an unkempt coat and a rapid heart rate. Many cats also lose muscle, and some show behavioral changes such as irritability. A minority of cats are instead quiet and eat poorly. Signs usually develop slowly, and owners may mistake them for normal aging.

### Diagnosis

Diagnosis is based on a blood test measuring the thyroid hormone thyroxine (total T4), which we can run in our own clinic laboratory. A raised T4 together with typical signs confirms the diagnosis. In early or mild cases, or when the cat has another illness at the same time, T4 can still be within the normal range. In that case, the test is repeated a couple of weeks or more later, or free T4 is measured together with total T4. Free T4 is never interpreted on its own, because it can be falsely high in cats with other illnesses. If doubt remains, further tests such as a T3 suppression test or thyroid scintigraphy can help. During the examination, the vet may feel an enlarged thyroid gland in the neck. Blood pressure, the heart, kidney values and a urine sample are checked at the same time.

### Complications

Untreated hyperthyroidism makes the heart work harder and can thicken the heart muscle, in severe cases leading to heart failure. These changes can improve once the thyroid is under control, but some cats also have a separate heart disease that does not resolve. Up to about one in four hyperthyroid cats has high blood pressure. It can damage the eyes (in severe cases causing sudden blindness), kidneys, heart and brain. Blood pressure can stay high, or even rise for the first time, after the thyroid is treated, so it is checked before and during treatment. There is also an important link with kidney disease: hyperthyroidism increases blood flow through the kidneys and their filtration rate, and muscle loss lowers creatinine, a kidney value. Together, these can hide existing kidney disease that only shows up once the thyroid is treated — in one large study, this happened in about one in six cats. Leaving the thyroid untreated does not protect the kidneys; over time it damages them further. Over-treatment, where the thyroid hormone level falls too low, can also strain the kidneys. That is why kidney values are monitored closely after treatment begins.

### Treatment Options

There are four treatment options: daily medication, surgery, radioactive iodine and an iodine-restricted diet. We will help you choose the best option for your cat’s situation.

### Daily medication

The medicine, thiamazole (also known as methimazole), is given every day as tablets (e.g., Felimazole) or an oral solution (e.g., Apelka). It is relatively inexpensive, but the treatment is lifelong. Most cats tolerate it well. Side effects usually appear in the first weeks and seldom after two to three months. They include vomiting, poor appetite, lethargy or severe itching of the head and neck that can cause scratch wounds. Rarely, the liver or blood cells are affected, so contact us if your cat becomes unwell or feverish, turns yellowish or bleeds easily. T4, kidney values and blood counts are checked about 3, 6, 10 and 20 weeks after starting and after every dose change, then every few months.

### Handling the medicine safely at home

Thiamazole may harm an unborn child. Wash your hands after giving the medicine and after handling the cat’s litter or vomit, and do not split or crush the tablets. Women who could become pregnant should wear disposable gloves when giving the medicine and handling litter or vomit. If you are pregnant, may be pregnant or are planning a pregnancy, let someone else give the medicine and clean the litter tray.

### Surgery

Surgery (thyroidectomy) can cure the disease. In about 70 % of cats, both thyroid lobes are affected, and removing both can damage the nearby parathyroid glands and cause low blood calcium, which may be temporary or permanent. The cat is first stabilized with medication, because anesthesia carries extra risk in an untreated hyperthyroid cat.

### Radioactive iodine

Radioactive iodine (I-131) is considered the treatment of choice for most cats: a single treatment cures more than 95 %. In Finland, it is offered by Vet4Cat in Renko (Hämeenlinna) and Evidensia Tammisto Animal Hospital in Vantaa. The cat stays in isolation in the hospital for several days. For about two weeks after returning home, it must be kept indoors, and children and pregnant women must not be in contact with it. The treating clinic gives detailed instructions, including how to handle the cat’s feces. Before surgery or radioactive iodine, a trial period on medication can help predict how the kidneys will cope once the thyroid is controlled.

### Iodine-restricted diet

This prescription diet (Hill’s y/d) works only if the cat eats nothing else — not even treats, other pets’ food or prey — and even then not in every cat. Some cats also refuse it because of the taste. It is therefore suitable mainly for indoor cats in single-cat homes.

### Sources
